[MUJAHID:v1p108/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid interprets the three qurūʾ as three menstrual periods.
[MUJAHID:v1p108/r2] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | The concealed matter is pregnancy: a woman must not claim she is not pregnant when she is, or pregnant when she is not.
[MUJAHID:v1p108/r3] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid takes “during that” to mean during the waiting period.
[MUQATIL:2:228/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | A divorced woman who menstruates waits for three menstrual periods; Muqatil takes qurūʾ to mean menstruations.
[MUQATIL:2:228/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | What God created in their wombs means a child; belief in God’s oneness and the resurrection entails not concealing it.
[MUQATIL:2:228/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | The husband has the stronger right to take his wife back while she is pregnant; the verse concerns Ismaʿil al-Ghifari and his wife, who did not know she was pregnant.
[MUQATIL:2:228/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | For reconciliation, Ismaʿil revoked the divorce while his wife was pregnant; she gave birth, then she and the child died.
[MUQATIL:2:228/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Women have rights from their husbands corresponding to the rights their husbands have over them, in fairness.
[MUQATIL:2:228/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Men have an advantage in rights over women; God is mighty and wise in His merciful ruling concerning pregnancy.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For three-consonant nouns on the فَعْل pattern, the small-count plural through ten is normally أفعل.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An أفعال form can serve for larger numbers too, making a separate high-count pattern unnecessary, as with أقتاب and أرسان.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Weak-final nouns generally follow the same plural patterns, though particular forms and limits depend on attested usage.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Doubled nouns likewise use أفعال forms such as ألباب and أمداد; this may be their only attested plural pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For another uncommon three-letter pattern, the small-count plural is أفعال; its low frequency limits extension to other patterns.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms such as النمور and الوعول are rare analogies to الأسود rather than the regular pattern for this class.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Arabs say ثلاثة قروء in place of the expected small-count form ثلاثة أقرؤ; this is the plural form used in the verse.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some nouns use a feminine-ended plural such as قردة for a small count instead of the expected form أقراد.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Another three-consonant class takes أفعال for small counts and often فعول or فعال for larger counts, with فعول more frequent.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For nouns on فعلة such as قصعة, small counts take the feminine suffix with fatḥa; larger counts usually use فعال.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Above ten, this noun class commonly forms plurals on فعال or فعول.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The larger-count pattern for that class is فعال, though some nouns instead form plurals on فعول.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The feminine suffix can also denote a large number, as Ḥassān ibn Thābit’s الجفنات line shows.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Weak-final nouns in this class follow the same patterns, including forms in ركوة and قشوة.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Another feminine noun pattern has both a suffixed small-count form and a larger broken plural, as in رحبات and رحاب.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nouns on فعلة take a suffixed plural with ḍamma on the middle consonant for small counts, then commonly a broken plural on فعل.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some nouns of that class also form larger-count plurals on فعال; dialects may open the middle vowel in the suffixed plural.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A cited line attests the dialectal opening of the middle vowel in this plural.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Weak-final wāw nouns use parallel suffixed and broken plurals, as in خطوة/خطوات/خطى and عروة/عروات/عرى.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f28] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Weak-final yāʾ nouns often use the larger-count form without the feminine suffix, avoiding yāʾ after ḍamma.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f29] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A plural may be used directly after a numeral without a feminine numeral form, as in ثلاث غرف and ركب.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some nouns allow both فعول and فعال, while فعيل plurals such as الكليب and العبيد are rare.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f30] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Geminated nouns pattern like ركبة; their doubled consonant stays intact in forms such as سرر and جدد.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f31] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For feminine nouns on فعلة, small counts add the feminine suffix with kasra on the middle consonant; some dialects instead open it.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f32] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Larger-count forms are bare plurals such as سدر and قرب; speakers may use them for small numbers because this class rarely takes the suffix.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f33] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Weak-final yāʾ and wāw forms avoid the suffixed plural after kasra, as in لحية/لحى and فرية/فرى.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f34] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Doubled nouns in this class form both suffixed and broken plurals, as in قدة/قدات/قدد and ربة/ربات/ربب.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f35] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أفعل plurals such as أنعم and أشد occur but are rare and nonbasic.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f36] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Without the feminine suffix, some feminine nouns form plurals on فعل, as in تخمة/تخم and تهمة/تهم; this differs from masculine رطب.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أفعال sometimes replaces أفعل in this class; the cited al-Aʿshā line witnesses أزناد.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A plural on فعلة occurs as a nonbasic alternative, as in جبء/جبأة, فقع/فقعة, and قعب/قعبة.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Khalīl explains forms such as الفحالة and البعولة as adding feminine marking; other patterns are learned by transmission and analogy.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | خمسة كلاب can mean five individual members of the dog kind, like using كلاب for a dog's sound or رمان for its seed.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Three-letter nouns on the فَعَل pattern take أفعال for small counts.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتكسيرالواحدللجمع)#654/f9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For larger counts in that class, فعال is more common than فعول; other nouns use فعلان forms.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh says assimilation and clear articulation vary in acceptability with articulatory similarity; clarity improves as points of articulation grow farther apart.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With hāʾ and ḥāʾ, clear articulation is preferable, though assimilation is good because the two are close and share voiceless softness.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For ʿayn followed by hāʾ, clarity is preferable; assimilation is possible after changing the adjacent sounds to ḥāʾ, so assimilation occurs between like sounds.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With ʿayn and ḥāʾ, both clear articulation and assimilation are good because they share a point of articulation.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For ghayn and khāʾ, clarity is preferable though assimilation is acceptable; in the reverse order, clarity is better because ghayn is voiced.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With qāf and kāf, both assimilation and clarity are good; clarity is preferable for kāf before qāf because these are the tongue consonants nearest the throat.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Jīm and shīn may be either assimilated or articulated clearly because they share the middle-tongue articulation point.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Lām assimilates into rāʾ most naturally: their articulation points are close and both share a lateral quality.

d. 180 · author | holds | Nūn assimilates into rāʾ, with or without nasalization, because their articulation points are close and both are tongue consonants.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nūn assimilates into lām either with nasalization retained or without it; keeping nasalization preserves nūn's nasal sound.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nūn assimilates into mīm because their sounds are alike and both are voiced; their shared nasal resonance outweighs their different articulation points.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Hamza does not assimilate into a neighbor or receive assimilation, because its characteristic heaviness is handled by alteration or deletion.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Before bāʾ, nūn changes to mīm rather than bāʾ: mīm shares nūn's sound and bāʾ's articulation place, while bāʾ lacks nasal resonance.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nūn assimilates into wāw with or without nasalization, but does not become mīm because wāw is a soft, extended sound unlike mīm.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nūn assimilates into yāʾ with or without nasalization: yāʾ resembles wāw and is close to rāʾ, which itself is close to nūn.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Before other oral consonants, nūn may be a hidden sound articulated through the nose; this is lighter and remains identifiable because no other sound comes from that place.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When nūn is assimilated with nasalization into rāʾ, lām, yāʾ, or wāw, its articulation stays oral and only takes on nasal resonance.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nūn remains clearly articulated before hamza and the five throat consonants because they are distant from it and do not belong to its articulation class.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A hidden nūn does not assimilate into following throat consonants, nor do they become nūn, because they are distant and unlike it.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When nūn and mīm occur within one word, they are clearly distinguished, as are nūn before wāw and yāʾ, to avoid confusion with a geminate form.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r28] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl analyzes the derived form from wajila as awjal, by analogy with amḥā, because the added nūn occurs in a pattern without a doubled wāw.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r29] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nūn before rāʾ or lām is not normally left clear because the nearby articulation makes clarity heavy; assimilation risks confusion with genuine gemination.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Alif does not assimilate even with a neighboring alif: doing so would change both long vowels into other sounds, so it also resists nearby consonants.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r30] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Definite-article lām must assimilate before thirteen consonants, including ṭāʾ; this rule accounts for the assimilated lām in al-muṭallaqāt.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r31] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The article lām's obligatory assimilation set comprises eleven tongue-tip consonants plus ḍād and shīn, whose articulation extends toward neighboring places.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r32] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With lām outside the definite article, assimilation into rāʾ is preferable because rāʾ is closest and most similar; clear articulation remains valid in Hijazi speech.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r33] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Assimilation of non-article lām into ṭāʾ, dāl, tāʾ, ṣād, zāy, or sīn is allowed but less natural than before rāʾ because these sounds are farther away.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r34] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Lām assimilation into ẓāʾ, thāʾ, or dhāl is allowed but weaker; it is weaker still with ḍād and shīn, though connected articulation permits it.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r35] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Ṭarīf's verse attests to non-article lām assimilating into shīn, producing hīshiʾ for hal shayʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r38] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · مزاحم العقيلي | reports | Muzāḥim al-ʿUqaylī's verse witnesses lām assimilated into tāʾ, giving hataʿīn for hal taʿīn.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r39] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nūn is the least suitable target for lām assimilation, since nūn assimilates into lām and several other consonants, making the reverse pattern awkward.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Long yāʾ or wāw after fatḥa resist assimilation into adjacent consonants, because this would turn a sound with length and softness into one without them.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A following consonant cannot assimilate into a long yāʾ, since that would introduce softness into a sound that lacks it.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Mīm does not assimilate into bāʾ: when nūn changes before bāʾ, speakers choose mīm, so mīm is already the sound they turn to.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Fāʾ does not assimilate into bāʾ because of their articulation; bāʾ can assimilate into fāʾ through proximity and oral-consonant assimilation.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Rāʾ resists assimilation into lām or nūn because its trill and spread would be impaired; lām and nūn may assimilate into rāʾ without that loss.
[SIBAWAYH:هذابابالإدغامفيالحروفالمتقاربةالتيهيمنمخرجواحد#808/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Shīn does not assimilate into jīm because its extended, diffuse articulation makes the change objectionable; jīm may assimilate into shīn.
[FARRA:v1p145/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · عبد الله | reports | Ibn Masʿūd’s reading has the form raddatahunna in place of raddihinna.
[MAJAZ:v1p74/r1] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Buʿūlatuhunna means their husbands; its singular is baʿl.
[MAJAZ:v1p74/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Darajah means rank or status.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p92#3/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says women had concealed pregnancy so they could attribute the child to another man; God forbade this.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p92#3/r2] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says husbands have the stronger right to take their wives back during the waiting period.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p92#3/r3] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda explains the men’s degree as a degree of merit over women.
[AKHFASH:v1p187#2/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Qurūʾ is prolonged and hamzated, singular qurʾ is lightly hamzated, and aqraʾa al-marʾa means she became menstruating; the form also describes having had one or two periods.
[AKHFASH:v1p187#2/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | A qurʾ is the cessation of menstruation.
[AKHFASH:v1p187#2/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · بعضهم | reports | Some instead define a qurʾ as the interval between two menstruations.
[AKHFASH:v1p187#2/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · الشاعر | reports | An unnamed poet uses qaraʾa janīnan for not conceiving, supporting the root's pregnancy-related usage.
[AKHFASH:v1p187#2/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · الشاعر | reports | A second unnamed poet uses al-maqrāh for a watercourse, without hamza; it is unrelated to qurʾ in this sense.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p86/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Qurūʾ can mean menstruations or periods of purity; its singular is qurʾ and another plural is aqrāʾ.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p86/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Al-Aʿshā's verse uses qurūʾ for pure intervals, since travel for raids kept him from visiting his wives.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p86/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · النبي صلى الله عليه وعلى آله وسلم | reports | The Prophet's instruction that a woman with irregular bleeding abstain from prayer during her aqraʾ means her menstruation days.

[TAB-FULL:v4p95/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · آخرون | reports | Other authorities hold that qurūʾ in this verse means periods of purity rather than menstruation.
[TAB-FULL:v4p95/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عائشة | reports | Several reports attribute to Aisha the view that qurūʾ means periods of purity, not menstruation.
[TAB-FULL:v4p95/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عائشة | reports | Aisha says a divorced woman is separated from her husband and may marry again upon entering her third menstruation.
[TAB-FULL:v4p95/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عمرة وعائشة | reports | Al-Zuhri reports Amra's statement that Aisha understood qurʾ as purity, not menstruation.
[TAB-FULL:v4p95/r9] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو بكر بن عبد الرحمن وابن عمر | reports | Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman and Ibn Umar are reported to share the positions attributed here to Zayd and Aisha.
[TAB-FULL:v4p97/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · زيد بن ثابت | reports | Zayd ibn Thabit says that entering the third menstruation ends the marriage bond and permits her to marry again; al-Zuhri issued fatwas according to this view.
[TAB-FULL:v4p97/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عائشة | reports | Yahya ibn Saʿid reports Aisha's view that qurūʾ means periods of purity.
[TAB-FULL:v4p97/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · زيد بن ثابت وعلي بن أبي طالب | reports | Zayd says no return is allowed once the third menstruation begins, whereas Ali allows return until she washes after it.
[TAB-FULL:v4p97/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · زيد بن ثابت | reports | Zayd says the spouses no longer inherit from one another once she enters her third menstruation.
[TAB-FULL:v4p97/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · زيد بن ثابت ومعاوية بن أبي سفيان وابن عمر | reports | In the case of al-Ahwas, Muawiya asked Zayd whether a husband who died while his divorced wife was in her third period left her an inheritance; Zayd said no, and Ibn Umar held the same rule.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p301/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The feminine noun ṭāliq is used without tāʾ in ṭāliq, while ṭallaqat al-marʾatu and ṭuliqat are also reported forms.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p301/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · قوم | rejects | Some claim the feminine tāʾ is omitted from ṭāliq because the word only applies to women; Zajjāj rejects this since many shared masculine-feminine descriptors lack tāʾ.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p301/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · سيبويه وأصحابه | reports | Sībawayh and his colleagues analyze ṭāliq as a masculine-form adjective applied to a feminine noun, underlyingly something divorced or dhāt ṭalāq, like descriptors meaning a bearer of sons, daughters, or a child.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p301/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | When ṭāliq is derived directly from the verb, the feminine form is ṭāliqa; al-Aʿshā's verse addresses a woman as ṭāliqa.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p301/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · أهل الكوفة | reports | The Kufans understand qurūʾ as menstrual periods.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p301/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · أهل الحجاز ومالك | reports | The Hijazis and Mālik understand qurūʾ as periods of purity.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p301/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · أم سلمة | reports | The Kufans cite Umm Salama's report about Fāṭima bint Abī Ḥubays: she was told to wait through her menstrual days and wash outside them.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p301/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · النبي | reports | A second report says when Fāṭima's qurʾ arrives she should not pray; after it passes she should purify herself and pray until the next qurʾ.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p301/r9] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Aṣmaʿī says qurʾ means menstruation and aqraʾat al-marʾatu means she menstruated, strengthening the Kufan interpretation.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p305/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Qurʾ conveys gathering: it can mean blood gathering in the body during purity or gathering in the womb during menstruation, so both juristic interpretations are sound and the distinction reconciles them; miqraʾa and miqraʾ also name containers where water or provisions gather.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p305/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · قيل | reports | One view says women must not conceal a pregnancy, since doing so could assign the child to someone other than its father.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p305/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · قوم | reports | Another view identifies what is concealed as menstruation; Zajjāj prefers the child interpretation because God's creation in wombs more directly suggests the child, as other verses describe forming people there. | mentions 3:6, 23:14
[ZAJJAJ:v1p305/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The condition means that belief in God's threats and punishment for grave sins should restrain them from concealment, just as one tells an unjust person that faith should keep him from oppression.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p306/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Buʿūlāt is the plural of baʿl, like dhakar/dhukūra and ʿamm/ʿumūma.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p306/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The added feminine ending emphasizes a group; such forms occur only in usages attested by linguists, not freely by analogy.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p306/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Here means during the waiting period: husbands may take their wives back before the three qurūʾ end if they intend reconciliation.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p306/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Women have corresponding rights to those owed by them, according to God's commands on a husband's rights over his wife; this is bi-l-maʿrūf.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p307/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Men have an added prerogative: both sexes receive pleasure from the other, while the man's distinction is his spending and care for her. | mentions 4:34
[ZAJJAJ:v1p307/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | God is sovereign to judge and test as He wills, yet His legislation and trials always proceed with consummate wisdom.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p414#2/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أسماء بنت يزيد | reports | Asmāʾ bint Yazīd says divorced women initially had no waiting period; when she was divorced, God revealed the waiting period, first revealed for her.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p414#2/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عائشة | reports | ʿĀʾisha says qurūʾ means periods of purity.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p414#2/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · زيد بن ثابت وابن عمر وابن عباس وسالم بن عبد الله والقاسم بن محمد وعروة بن الزبير وسليمان بن يسار وأبو بكر بن عبد الرحمن وعطاء وقتادة والزهري | reports | Abū Muḥammad reports these authorities share ʿĀʾisha's gloss of purity periods.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p414#2/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عمر وعبد الله | reports | ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar consider a woman divorced once or twice still his wife until the time she may pray.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p414#2/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid interprets the three qurūʾ as three menstruations.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p414#2/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · علي وابن عباس وأبو الدرداء وعبادة بن الصامت وأبو موسى وسعيد بن جبير و

الحسن وعكرمة والشعبي وقتادة والربيع بن أنس ومقاتل بن حيان والسدي وعطاء الخراساني | reports | Abū Muḥammad reports these authorities also interpret qurūʾ as menstruations; Qatāda held this in one report.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p414#2/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | A pregnant divorced woman hid her pregnancy until birth; ʿUmar identified her as concealing what God created in her womb.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p414#2/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · محمد بن كعب القرظي والسدي والنخعي وقتادة ومقاتل بن حيان | reports | These authorities explain what is concealed as pregnancy; al-Nakhaʿī held this in one view.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p415/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar says a woman may not conceal pregnancy or menstruation.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p415/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس والشعبي والحكم بن عتيبة ومجاهد والربيع بن أنس والضحاك | reports | These authorities are reported to include both pregnancy and menstruation.

[IBNABIHATIM:v2p415/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd tells a Bedouin that his nephew may not take back a wife who hid pregnancy until birth, asking what he wants with a woman who does not believe.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p415/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd glosses belief in the Last Day as belief in the unseen in which deeds are requited.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p415/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says a husband divorcing his pregnant wife once or twice may take her back until delivery.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p415/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد والحسن وإبراهيم النخعي وعكرمة والضحاك والربيع بن أنس وقتادة ومقاتل بن حيان وزيد بن أسلم | reports | These authorities are reported to share Ibn ʿAbbās's ruling on taking back a pregnant wife before delivery.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p417/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās likes to adorn himself for his wife as he likes her to adorn herself for him.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p417/r10] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أبو العالية والربيع بن أنس | reports | Abū al-ʿĀliya and al-Rabīʿ say it is might in vengeance.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p417/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مقاتل بن حيان | reports | Muqātil says women have rights corresponding to their duties in fairness.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p417/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās does not want to claim all his due from his wife.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p417/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid calls the degree God's favor to men, including jihad, inheritance, and other privileges.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p417/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أبو مالك عن السدي | reports | Al-Suddī says a man may divorce her and she has no say in that matter.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p417/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · زيد بن أسلم | reports | Zayd ibn Aslam interprets the degree as authority.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p417/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says men have a degree of excellence over women.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p417/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مقاتل بن حيان | reports | Muqātil says the privilege reflects men's spending on women.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p417/r9] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الحسن وقتادة | reports | Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda explain God's might here as might in blessing.
[IBNABIHATIM:v2p418/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الضحاك عن ابن عباس | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk reports Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss of ḥakīm as one who makes firm whatever He wills.
[NAHHAS:v1p312/r4] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The tāʾ in ثلاثة أقراء counts a masculine noun; the singular is قرء. Sibawayh takes the estimate as three plural qurūʾ because he treats that plural as one for many.
[NAHHAS:v1p312/r5] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | rejects | The argument that tāʾ proves qurūʾ means purity rather than menstruation is a crude error: one thing can have masculine and feminine names, such as دار and منزل.
[NAHHAS:v1p312/r6] NAHHAS, d. 338 · إبراهيم النخعي | reports | He explains what God created in their wombs as menstruation; Nahhas calls this among the soundest views and concludes that قرء here means menstruation, not purity.
[NAHHAS:v1p312/r7] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | prefers | The womb evidence points to menstruation: no child is mentioned, and the relevant created thing is menstrual blood. Divorce is before the waiting term; since divorce occurs during purity, the following interval is menstruation. | mentions 65:1
[NAHHAS:v1p312/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The Arabic estimate for the waiting-period clause is ليعتددن, ‘so they may count their waiting period.’
[NAHHAS:v1p312/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | وبعولتهن أحق بردهن is subject and predicate; بعولة is the plural of بعل and its tāʾ marks a feminine collective.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p278/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The counted three qurūʾ cannot consist of two whole units plus part of a third, because an explicitly enumerated total requires three complete units.
[THALABI:v2p170/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · من قال بهذا القول | reports | Those who take qurʾ as menstruation say a divorced woman remains in her waiting period until the third menstruation ends; Ali says she cannot return to her husband until she bathes after it and prayer is permitted.
[THALABI:v2p170/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · زيد بن ثابت وابن عمر وعائشة | reports | Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Umar, Aisha, Malik, al-Shafii, and the people of Medina take qurʾ as periods of purity, using the divorce instruction in 65:1 and the Prophet's direction to Ibn Umar as evidence. | mentions 65:1
[THALABI:v2p170/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | When Ibn Umar divorced during menstruation, the Prophet told Umar to have him take her back, then divorce or keep her once she was pure, reciting 65:1 to show the waiting period starts in purity. | mentions 65:1
[THALABI:v2p170/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · علي | reports | Ali says a man who divorces his wife once or twice cannot return to her until she has bathed after the third menstruation and prayer is permitted.
[THALABI:v2p170/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · عائشة | reports | On the purity interpretation, Aisha says that once the divorced woman enters her third menstruation she is separated from her husband and may marry another; she explicitly defines qurʾ as purity, not menstruation.
[THALABI:v2p170/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر بن عبد الرحمن | reports | Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman says every jurist he encountered held Aisha's interpretation that the qurʾ are periods of purity.
[THALABI:v2p170/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The disagreement arises because qurʾ is a contronym: Arabic uses it for menstruation and for purity, with أقرأت said of a woman in either state.
[THALABI:v2p170/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو عمر وأبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Umar and Abu Ubayda derive qurʾ from a thing's appointed time of coming and going; al-A'sha's verse uses it of the purity missed while he campaigned away from his wives.
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The verse is phrased as a report but functions as a command, like the instruction that mothers nurse their children. | mentions 2:233
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | A husband may return his wife during her waiting period if he seeks reconciliation; he must not use repeated return near the end of the period to harm her.
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Women have rights over their husbands corresponding to the rights husbands have over them, according to proper custom.
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Asked about a wife's rights, the Prophet says her husband must not strike her face or insult her, must feed and clothe her as he does himself, and must not abandon her.
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | A menstruating divorcee waits three qurūʾ; a pregnant divorcee until delivery; a premenarchal or postmenopausal divorcee three months; pregnant widows until delivery, and other widows four months and ten days.
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Enslaved women's applicable waiting periods are half of a free woman's, so their menstrual waiting period is two qurūʾ; an unconsummated divorce entails no waiting period.
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · عكرمة وإبراهيم | reports | Ikrima and Ibrahim take what God created in the wombs to mean menstrual blood.
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس وقتادة ومقاتل | reports | Ibn Abbas, Qatada, and Muqatil take the phrase to mean a child, that is, pregnancy.
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Women must not hide menstruation or pregnancy to defeat a husband's right of return or a child's claim; a woman is trusted about her sexual parts.
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Buʿūla means husbands, plural of baʿl; baʿl originally means master or owner, and the husband is so called for managing his wife's affairs. The verse about worshipping Baal is cited. | mentions 37:125
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · مسلم بن محارب | reports | Muslim ibn Muharib reads the tāʾ in buʿūlatuhunna with sukūn because of the succession of vowelled sounds.
[THALABI:v2p171#2/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · author | prefers | Thaʿlabī prefers the usual vocalized form as more eloquent, fitting, and sound.
[THALABI:v2p171/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · مالك بن الحارث الهذلي | reports | Malik ibn al-Harith al-Hudhali uses قاري for an appointed time, saying winds blow at their time.
[THALABI:v2p171/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The source says the stars are said to أقرأت when they rise and when they set, further illustrating recurrent times.
[THALABI:v2p171/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · كثير | reports | Kathir's line uses أقرأت of the Pleiades setting, showing another recurrent appointed time.
[THALABI:v2p171/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | On this

[THALABI:v2p171/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · قيل | reports | An alternative etymology derives qurʾ from gathering; it compares the term with water collected in a basin and a womb enclosing a fetus.
[THALABI:v2p171/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · عمرو بن كلثوم | reports | Amr ibn Kulthum's line uses لم تقرأ جنينا for a woman who has not conceived or gathered an embryo in her womb; Arabs say a camel has not gathered a fetus.
[THALABI:v2p171/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · الزجاج | prefers | Al-Zajjaj chooses this etymology and connects it to qara'tu water in a basin; qurʾ is retained, gathered blood in either purity or menstruation, with purity preferred because it holds blood back while menstruation releases it.
[THALABI:v2p171/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | prefers | Qurʾ is blood held together: it can describe menstruation or purity, but purity is stronger because it gathers and retains blood while menstruation releases it.
[THALABI:v2p172/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet urges kind treatment of women, describing them as dependent wards entrusted to husbands by God's trust and made lawful through God's word.
[THALABI:v2p172/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A woman representing women asks about their reward when men fight and die; the Prophet replies that obedience to husbands and recognition of their rights equal that service, though few women do so.
[THALABI:v2p172/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In a report from Maimuna, the Prophet praises spouses who serve one another: wives who comply except in sin receive the stated reward of a thousand martyrs, and gentle husbands the reward of a hundred.
[THALABI:v2p172/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Answering Umar, the Prophet says women may surpass men in reward, a wife's contentment and prayer elevate her husband, and betraying him is grave after shirk; he warns about orphans and women and equates wives' rights with his own.
[THALABI:v2p172/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Thaʿlabī glosses the men's degree over women as superiority in merit.
[THALABI:v2p172/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains the degree by the dowry and financial support a man provides his wife.
[THALABI:v2p172/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · قيل | reports | One reported view explains the degree as a difference in intellect.
[THALABI:v2p172/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · قيل | reports | Another reported view explains the degree by inheritance.
[THALABI:v2p172/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · قيل | reports | A further reported view says the degree itself is the explanation.
[THALABI:v2p172/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · قتادة | reports | Qatada identifies the men's degree with jihad.
[THALABI:v2p173/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · أنس | reports | Anas reports that women came to the Prophet saying men had gained virtue through jihad and asking what deed remained for women in God's path.
[THALABI:v2p173/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Asked whether women have jihad, the Prophet calls their jihad guarding their zeal and struggling against themselves; patient women are fighters and garrisoned, with two rewards.
[THALABI:v2p173/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · قيل | reports | One view explains the men's degree as divorce and return.
[THALABI:v2p173/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · قيل | reports | Another view explains the degree as testimony.
[THALABI:v2p173/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · قيل | reports | Another view explains the degree as strength in worship.
[THALABI:v2p173/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · سفيان وزيد بن أسلم | reports | Sufyan and Zayd ibn Aslam explain the degree as authority or governance.
[THALABI:v2p173/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · القتيبي | reports | Al-Qutaybi says the degree means a virtue or advantage concerning rights.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p290/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Divorced women are those whose marital ties have been released; talaq means release, like a sheep left without a shepherd.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p290/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | One etymology derives quruʾ from gathering: the Qur'an gathers letters, and Arabic uses the root for food collected in the mouth and water collected in a pool.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p290/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Another derivation compares talaq to a horse running a stretch without restraint: the woman is released after previously being forbidden to others.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p290/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | A wife is said to be in her husband's bond because she is as if tied to something.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p290/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Talaqat al-mar'a can instead mean she gave birth; that sense comes from ṭalaq, the pain of childbirth, not divorce.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p290/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The waiting period is the span of three qurūʾ, whose meaning is disputed.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p291/r22] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · حميد | reports | Humayd says the degree is that men have beards.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p291/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Arabic expressions about a need coming due, a star setting or rising, and a wind blowing in its season illustrate quruʾ as a due time.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p291/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | On the time derivation, quruʾ means menses because it is the regular time for blood to flow, or purity because it is the time for blood to be withheld.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p208/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-mutallaqat are women released from their husbands' bonds; the verse concerns adult, consummated, nonpregnant divorcees whose waiting period is being explained.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p216/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The womb is the place where a child originates and the vessel that holds it in the abdomen.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p216/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس وقتادة ومقاتل | reports | Ibn Abbas, Qatada, and Muqatil interpret it as pregnancy and the child; concealment could defeat a husband's right of return or the child's rights. | mentions 3:6

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p216/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · عطاء عن ابن عباس | reports | Ata reports from Ibn Abbas that a wicked wife may conceal pregnancy because she longs for her husband and wants to prolong the waiting period; a pregnant woman's period ends at childbirth. | mentions 22:5
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p217/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | This means that a believer is expected to act this way; the obligation is not limited to believers alone.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p218/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Baʿula is a collective plural of baʿl, like fuḥula, dhukura, khuʾula, and ʿumuma; its feminine tāʾ reinforces the group's grammatical femininity and is only used in attested forms.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p218/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | A woman praised for good tabaʿʿul treats her husband well; the author also cites a hadith about women excelling in their treatment of husbands.

[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p101/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · النبي | reports | Jurjānī cites a Prophetic saying comparing one who teaches good but does not practice it to a lamp that lights others while consuming itself; he also gives a wick variant and states no grading.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p101/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Parables strengthen meanings by moving the listener from what is hidden to what is clear and from abstract reasoning to familiar sensory or innate knowledge, which feels firmer and more certain.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p101/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | He illustrates this method with concrete admonitions: one cannot harvest grapes from thorns, one reaps what one sows, pearls should not be cast before swine, and worldly life is a passing shadow or borrowed garment, with al-Shāfiʿī and Labīd cited.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p244/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The poem personifies separation as a discerning rival who keeps the lovers apart out of jealousy, turning estrangement into a deliberate act with an imagined motive.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p244/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The red eye is real, but its supposed redness from blood spilled by beauties is an invented cause; Jurjānī identifies Ibn al-Muʿtazz as the originator of this conceit.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p244/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | This differs from saying the wind envies the speaker: the wind really blows his cloak onto his face, while envy is the invented cause; the eye image instead invents a cause for an existing condition.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p244/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Other poets reinterpret illness and fever as keen insight, minds ablaze, and strong resolve; Jurjānī treats this as an imaginative reinterpretation of a quality, without a separate cause-and-effect fiction.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p400/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | After mentioning a possessed noun, eloquence favors repeating the possessor’s explicit name instead of replacing it with a pronoun, whose use weakens the effect.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p400/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Al-Sahib argues that the verse needs ‘sword’ repeated four times; replacing the latter instances with pronouns would spoil its quality, though not its meter.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p400/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | He cites Dibil’s repeated ʿAmr, an unnamed poet’s repeated ‘wood’, and al-Mutanabbi’s repeated ‘time’ as evidence that explicit repetition can be more graceful than pronouns.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p400/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | rejects | Ambiguity does not explain the preference for an explicit noun: a plural example remains stylistically awkward even when the pronoun cannot be confused with another referent.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p400/r5] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · أبو يعقوب | reports | In an anecdote related to al-Jahiz, Abu Yaqub says indirect allusion does not affect understanding in the way explicit disclosure does; the author uses this to explain the force of repetition.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p400/r6] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The explicit repetitions in ‘By the truth We sent it down, and by the truth it descended’ and ‘God, the One, God, the Eternal’ create an effect that pronouns would lose. | mentions 17:105, 112:1, 112:2
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p400/r7] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | He introduces a Hamasa poem as another instance of the same point, saying it resembles Ibn al-Rumi’s example because it too is a simile.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p51/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Studying why expression is eloquent has religious value: it helps prevent errors about revelation and interpretation and equips readers to give a persuasive argument for a Qur'anic verse.

[JISHUMI:v1p906#2/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الأصمعي والأخفش والفراء والكسائي | reports | One proposed origin is gathering: blood gathers in the womb, hence menstruation is called a qurʾ; examples include stars gathering at setting and a basin gathering water.

[JISHUMI:v1p909/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · القتبي وأبو مسلم | reports | Al-Qutbi and Abu Muslim explain the degree as a special privilege in rights.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r16] JISHUMI, d. 494 · القاضي | prefers | Al-Qadi says the verse can encompass all of the reported explanations.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r17] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | God is powerful, nothing can prevent Him, and wise in that He does only what is good.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r18] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | Another explanation takes al-ḥakīm to mean that God knows everything.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r19] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Although phrased as a statement, the verse means a command: the divorced woman is legally bound to observe the waiting period.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | For a believer, this is the proper rule and characteristic, and she should not act against it.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r20] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The waiting requirement applies to every divorced woman except those excluded by other evidence.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r21] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | A woman divorced before consummation has no waiting period, as stated in 33:49. | mentions 33:49
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r22] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | One view treats the waiting-period rule as specified by the verse in al-Ahzab. | mentions 33:49
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r23] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | Another view says the rule for women divorced before consummation is abrogated; the author prefers this because delaying clarification past the time of address is impermissible. | mentions 33:49
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Husbands have the superior right to restore their wives while the wives remain in the waiting period.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The phrase refers to the time of menstruation and the waiting period; reconciliation means observing God's obligations and avoiding harm such as prolonging the wait.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Wives and husbands each have corresponding rights, especially in good companionship and avoiding harm.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The required obedience of wives is what is recognized as the husband's lawful right over them.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | Another explanation takes maʿrūf as good, beautiful conduct that accords with the law.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس | reports | One view understands men's degree as superiority or merit.
[JISHUMI:v1p909/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | Another view ties men's degree to the dowry they provide and their spending on wives.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The rule concerns women who menstruate; postmenopausal women and girls are covered instead by the three-month rule, and enslaved women are outside this verse's three-cycle count.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The husband alone may revoke during the waiting period; he needs neither his wife's consent nor a new contract or witnesses.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Reconciliation is required for the return to be proper, but not for its legal effects to take hold; the community agrees that a harmful return still has those effects, as with divorce during menstruation.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Each spouse has rights corresponding to those of the other, especially in marital companionship; the author calls this a remarkably concise statement.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Divorce is limited to three for a free man with a free wife and two for an enslaved woman married to an enslaved man.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa counts the number of divorces by the wife: an enslaved wife has a limit of two.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi‘i counts the number of divorces by the husband.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r16] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The prescribed time for divorce is a period of purity in which the husband has not had intercourse with her; divorce during menstruation is disliked.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r17] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa considers a triple divorce pronounced at once to be a sinful innovation that nevertheless takes effect.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r18] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi‘i permits pronouncing three divorces at once.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r19] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قوم | reports | Some jurists count a triple divorce pronounced at once as one divorce.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | A woman may not conceal menstruation or pregnancy, and her statement about it is accepted, since otherwise the prohibition would have no purpose.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r20] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قوم | reports | Other jurists say a triple divorce pronounced at once does not take effect.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Concealing these facts to harm the husband is prohibited.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Anyone who knows a religious ruling may not hide it; forbidding concealment of menstruation information makes concealment of religious teachings even more clearly forbidden.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The reference to husbands shows that marriage remains in effect, since divorce does not itself eliminate the right to revoke.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Divorce has an effect that a return can remove; scholars differ whether that effect is approach to final separation or prohibition of intercourse.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The right of return exists during the waiting period.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The passage also says that apostasy removes the effect established by divorce.
[JISHUMI:v1p910/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The right of return applies to a divorce short of the final divorce, as the next verse says she is not lawful after he divorces her again. | mentions 2:230
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | After three divorces, a woman cannot return to her former husband until she validly marries another man, consummates the marriage, and completes her waiting period.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو حنيفة والشافعي | reports | They hold that a later revocable divorce attaches to a prior revocable divorce, and an irrevocable divorce attaches to a revocable one, but an irrevocable divorce does not attach to another irrevocable divorce.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الهادي والزيدية | reports | Al-Hadi and the Zaydis say a further divorce does not attach to a divorced woman until the husband has taken her back, in every case.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa says a revocable divorce can attach to a prior irrevocable divorce.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi‘i says a revocable divorce does not attach to a prior irrevocable divorce.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | A waiting period is due for a consummated wife who is divorced or widowed, for an unconsummated wife if her husband dies, for intercourse by mistake or an invalid marriage, and for a freed or widowed umm walad.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | For the relevant umm walad and a menstruating divorced woman, the author gives the waiting period as three menstruations; al-Shafi‘i says one for the umm walad.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r16] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa counts qurūʾ as menstruations.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r17] JISHUMI, d. 494 · مالك والشافعي | reports | Malik and al-Shafi‘i count qurūʾ as the intervening periods of purity.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r18] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | The author prefers menstruation because the waiting period spans three complete cycles and because transfer to months when menstruation is absent shows menstruation is the norm.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r19] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The three-cycle rule applies to a menstruating, nonpregnant woman whose marriage was consummated.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Divorce is either revocable or irrevocable; an irrevocably divorced woman requires a new contract to return, while a revocable divorce allows return.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r20] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | A postmenopausal or young girl divorced after consummation waits three months.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r21] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | A widow waits four months and ten days whether or not her husband consummated the marriage.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r22] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | An enslaved woman's waiting period is half the free woman's term in months and two menstrual periods when counted by qurūʾ.
[JISHUMI:v1p912/r23] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو حنيفة | reports | If a husband divorces his wife while fatally ill and dies, and she inherits through his admission, Abu Hanifa requires the longer of the two waiting periods.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p305/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · زيد بن ثابت وغيره | reports | Zayd ibn Thabit and others share that view.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p305/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أشهب | reports | Ashhab says the bond and inheritance rights continue until bleeding is confirmed as menstruation, since it could be a nonmenstrual spot.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p305/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عمر ومجاهد والربيع وابن زيد والضحاك | reports | These exegetes understand what God created in the wombs to include menstruation and pregnancy.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p305/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The prohibition protects the husband from harm and preserves his right of revocation; false menstrual claims can defeat that right or impose unowed maintenance.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p305/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says pre-Islamic women concealed pregnancy to attribute a child to a new husband, and that the verse was revealed about this practice.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p305/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says husbands asked about pregnancy before divorcing to avoid harm to themselves and the child; God commanded truthfulness.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p305/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · إبراهيم النخعي وعكرمة | reports | Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Ikrima take the phrase to mean menstruation.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p306/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Ishaq explains the degree as maintenance and the husband's position as caretaker.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p306/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd takes the degree to mean the husband's control of the marital bond, including that divorce is in his hand.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p306/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · حميد | rejects | Humayd identifies the degree with the beard; Ibn Atiyya says this is weak if authentic and unsupported by the wording or meaning.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p306/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | prefers | The reported interpretations together imply male preference; Ibn Atiyya rejects the beard explanation as textually and semantically weak.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p306/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | God cannot be thwarted and is wise in the rulings and affairs He executes.
[TABRISI:2:228#2/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | In 37:125 baʿl means a lord or, alternatively, an idol; baʿl also names a palm watered by its roots. | mentions 37:125
[TABRISI:2:228#2/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | The competing view takes qurūʾ as menstruations, attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and also reported from ʿAlī; it is Abū Ḥanīfa's position.
[TABRISI:2:228#2/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو حنيفة وأصحابه | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa and his followers support the menstruation interpretation with a report that the Prophet told a woman to stop praying during her days of qurūʾ.
[TABRISI:2:228#2/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Related uses describe being constricted by a matter, acting arrogantly, or a bewildered woman; the root's underlying idea is superiority.
[TABRISI:2:228#2/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Rijāl and related forms derive from strength; daraja means rank or degree.
[TABRISI:2:228#2/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The conditional answer is omitted: if they believe, they will not conceal; the answer to the husbands' condition is likewise omitted and understood as their being entitled to return them.
[TABRISI:2:228#2/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The annexation in mithlu alladhī ʿalayhinna is not a true genitive construction because alladhī ʿalayhinna functions as its object.
[TABRISI:2:228#2/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The waiting-period rule concerns divorced women who have consummated marriage, menstruate, and are not pregnant; they wait until three qurūʾ pass and may not marry meanwhile.
[TABRISI:2:228#2/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The wording is grammatically declarative but functions as a command to wait.
[TABRISI:2:228#2/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | prefers | The author and the Imāmī position take qurūʾ as periods of purity; this is also attributed to Zayd ibn Thābit, ʿĀʾisha, Ibn ʿUmar, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and the people of Medina.
[TABRISI:2:228#2/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن شهاب | reports | Ibn Shihāb says all the people of his region held that the aqrāʾ are periods of purity except Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The cited instruction to a mustaḥāḍa to stop praying on her qurūʾ days supports the menstruation interpretation, since prayer is suspended during menstruation.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس وقتادة | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda take it to mean pregnancy.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عمر والحسن والصادق | prefers | Ibn ʿUmar, al-Ḥasan, and al-Ṣādiq include both menstruation and pregnancy; the author prefers this broader interpretation.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · الصادق | reports | Al-Ṣādiq says God entrusted women with three matters: menstruation, purity, and pregnancy.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says concealment would wrong the husband by preventing him from returning to his wife.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says concealment could falsely attribute a child to someone else, as in pre-Islamic practice.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The faith clause is not a legal condition permitting unbelievers to conceal; it warns that true faith prevents this sin.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | prefers | For the purity interpretation, the author cites 65:1, understood as ordering divorce during a pure period in which the couple has not had intercourse. | mentions 65:1
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · النبي | reports | When Ibn ʿUmar divorced his wife during menstruation, the Prophet told him to take her back and, once she was pure, either divorce or keep her. | mentions 65:1
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | prefers | The Prophet's recitation of 65:1 indicates that the waiting period begins with purity: a woman divorced during menstruation has not yet begun it. | mentions 65:1
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · ربيعة الرأي | reports | Rabīʿa al-Raʾy says the Qurʾānic aqrāʾ are the periods of purity between menstruations, not menstruations themselves.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو جعفر | reports | Al-Bāqir says Rabīʿa did not reach the view independently but received it from ʿAlī.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · علي | reports | ʿAlī says

 qurʾ is purity: blood gathers during that period and is expelled when menstruation comes; the waiting period ends upon entering the third menstruation.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · الباقر | rejects | Al-Bāqir rejects the Iraqi report that ʿAlī said a husband retains the right of return until the third menstruation has ended.
[TABRISI:2:228#3/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · إبراهيم وعكرمة | reports | Ibrāhīm and ʿIkrima take what is hidden in the wombs to mean menstruation.
[TABRISI:2:228#4/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | While the waiting period remains, husbands may restore their wives to the prior marital state; that right expires when the period ends.
[TABRISI:2:228#4/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | A husband alone may revoke a revocable divorce without his wife's consent, a new contract, or witnesses; the right applies only to revocable divorces although the opening is general.
[TABRISI:2:228#4/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Men used to divorce once, wait until the period nearly ended, revoke, and repeat the cycle before divorcing a third time, thereby harming the wife.
[TABRISI:2:228#4/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Revocation is permitted for reconciliation rather than harm, but this condition concerns permissibility, not legal effect; the community agrees the legal effects still apply when harm is intended.
[TABRISI:2:228#4/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | This concise principle gives women rights corresponding to their obligations, governed by accepted standards of decent treatment.
[TABRISI:2:228#4/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Women's rights include good companionship, freedom from harm, equitable division, maintenance, and clothing; the husband's include obedience, marital exclusivity, and preserving his paternity.
[TABRISI:2:228#4/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · النبي | reports | A report prompted by a woman identified as Muʿādh's wife says a husband must not strike his wife's face or insult her, and must feed and clothe her as he does himself and not abandon her.
[TABRISI:2:228#4/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · النبي | reports | The Prophet reminds men that they received women in God's trust; wives must preserve marital exclusivity, and husbands owe them customary maintenance and clothing, with any corrective strike non-injurious.
[TABRISI:2:228#5/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · مجاهد وقتادة | reports | Mujāhid and Qatāda say men's degree includes women's obedience, men's authority to dissolve the marriage, a larger inheritance share, and jihad.
[TABRISI:2:228#5/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reads the degree as a man's obligation to show extra generosity and not demand every right in full.
[TABRISI:2:228#5/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says women receive pleasure from men as men receive it from women, while men have a degree through spending and care.
[TABRISI:2:228#5/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · علي بن إبراهيم | reports | ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm's tafsir says men's rights over women are greater than women's rights over men.
[TABRISI:2:228#5/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · الباقر | reports | A report from al-Bāqir says a wife should obey her husband, seek permission for household charity, voluntary fasting, and leaving home, and not deny him sex; the husband's right is paramount, and the Prophet says he would have ordered prostration to him if it were permitted.
[TABRISI:2:228#6/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God is powerful over whatever He wills, cannot be prevented or overcome, and acts according to wisdom.
[TABRISI:2:228#6/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | One view says the rule is abrogated for a woman divorced before consummation and for a pregnant divorcee by 33:49 and 65:4. | mentions 33:49, 65:4
[TABRISI:2:228#6/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another view treats those two cases as specified exceptions to this verse rather than abrogated portions.
[TABRISI:2:228/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Qurūʾ has the few plural aqruʾ and the more commonly used aqraʾ or qurūʾ; the common plural form signals the many women governed by the rule although each waits three periods.
[TABRISI:2:228/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | One root sense of qurʾ is gathering, as with the gathering of letters in recitation or a womb gathering around a pregnancy.
[TABRISI:2:228/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · عمرو بن كلثوم | reports | ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm's line uses qaraʾ for a womb that has not gathered a fetus, illustrating the root sense of gathering.
[TABRISI:2:228/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | On the gathering sense, a woman is said to have aqraʾ when she menstruates as blood gathers in the womb; qurʾ can also mean purity as blood gathers in the body.
[TABRISI:2:228/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | A second root sense is a regularly recurring time, which can designate either menstruation or purity.
[TABRISI:2:228/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | A poet's line about the time when winds blow illustrates the sense of a regularly recurring time.
[TABRISI:2:228/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · الأعشى | reports | Al-Aʿshā's lines about his wives' qurūʾ use the term for periods of purity, supporting that interpretation.
[TABRISI:2:228/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Baʿūla is the plural of baʿl, husband; the husband is called this because he is above the woman through marital authority.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p188/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Ba'l can mean husband, companion, or lord; it can also refer to land watered by its own roots without rain.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p188/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · علي بن عبيد الله | reports | Ali ibn Ubayd Allah says a husband is called a woman's ba'l because she is like the field in which a child grows, and the man's fluid is its irrigation.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p188/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · قيل | reports | Another account derives ba'l from elevation: a husband is ba'l because he is above the woman.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p188/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | The first Qur'anic sense is husband, in the divorce verse and in Shu'ayb's wife calling him her husband. | mentions 11:72
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p188/r5] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | The second sense is the idol Ba'l, whom the people are asked whether they worship while abandoning the best of creators. | mentions 37:125
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p326/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Rijal is the plural of rajul and ordinarily names human males after puberty; some derive it from strength, and the entry notes related senses including strong walkers, spontaneous speech, combed hair, a walker, and a locust segment.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p326/r10] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | The ninth sense is husbands, as in the statement that men have a degree over women and are responsible for them. | mentions 4:34
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p326/r11] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | The tenth sense is males, in the statements that God spread many men and that Muhammad is not the father of any of the community's men. | mentions 4:1, 33:40
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p326/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | The first Qur'anic referent is messengers, as in the statement that only men were sent before Muhammad and received revelation. | mentions 21:7
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p326/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | A second referent is angels, in the men on the heights who recognize people by their marks. | mentions 7:46
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p326/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | The third referent is the Prophet's steadfast Companions in battle, who remained true to their covenant with God. | mentions 33:23
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p326/r5] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | A fourth referent is the people of Quba, praised for loving purification. | mentions 9:108
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p326/r6] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | A fifth referent is men who keep the appointed prayer times and are not distracted by trade. | mentions 24:37
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p326/r7] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | The sixth referent is oppressed believing men among the people of Mecca. | mentions 48:25
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p326/r8] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | The seventh referent is poor Muslims, whom the people of Hell say they once counted among the wicked. | mentions 38:62
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p326/r9] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | The eighth sense is people walking on foot, in the permission to pray on foot or mounted and the pilgrimage command to come walking. | mentions 2:239, 22:27
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p258#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that women manipulated pregnancy claims to secure or prevent their husbands' return; the practice continued into Islam and prompted the waiting-period ruling.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p258#2/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj derives the word from gathering: Qurʾan is recited as collected speech, while menstrual blood gathers in the body or womb; either account is possible.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p258#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The author says the divorce instruction in 65:1 was revealed first, followed by this waiting-period verse. | mentions 65:1
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p258#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari derives talaq from releasing a camel that had been tied; the woman's former marital bonds are likened to a tether that the husband releases.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p258#2/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Another linguist derives talaq from releasing something from one's hand and says frequent usage differentiates the form used for wives from the general verb “to release.”
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p258#2/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Quruʾ can mean either periods of purity or menstruation; the verb is used for both when a woman enters either state.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p258#

2/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · النبي | reports | The Prophet's instruction to a woman with irregular bleeding to sit through her quruʾ days uses quruʾ to mean menstruation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p258#2/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Al-Aʿsha's verse about missing the quruʾ of one's women uses the word for periods of purity while away on a campaign.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p258#2/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba says the root means a time or appointed period: both menstruation and purity occur at their proper times.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p258#2/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الشاعر الهذلي | reports | A Huthayli poet's phrase about winds returning to their qariʾ supports the sense of a recurrent time.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p259/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عمر، علي، ابن مسعود، أبو موسى، عبادة بن الصامت، أبو الدرداء، عكرمة، الضحاك، السدي، سفيان الثوري، الأوزاعي، الحسن بن صالح، أبو حنيفة وأصحابه، أحمد بن حنبل | reports | They interpret qurūʾ as menstruations; Ahmad says he once held that it meant clean intervals but now adopts menstruation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p259/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · زيد بن ثابت، ابن عمر، عائشة، الزهري، أبان بن عثمان، مالك بن أنس، الشافعي، أحمد بن حنبل | reports | They interpret qurūʾ as clean intervals; Ahmad had indicated this view before adopting menstruation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p259/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The declarative wording that divorced women wait functions as a command, like the command phrased as a report in 2:233; conversely, a command can be phrased as a report in 19:75. | mentions 2:233, 19:75
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p259/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Here the divorced women are adult women whose marriages were consummated and who are not pregnant.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p260/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عمر، ابن عباس، مجاهد، قتادة، مقاتل، ابن قتيبة، الزجاج | reports | One view is that what women must not conceal in their wombs is pregnancy.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p260/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عكرمة، عطية، النخعي، الزهري | reports | A second view identifies what must not be concealed as menstruation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p260/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عمر، ابن زيد | reports | A third view includes both pregnancy and menstruation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p260/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | The condition is phrased as a threat and emphasis, like telling a man, “If you are a believer, do not act unjustly.”
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p260/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | One reason for the threat is the husband's entitlement to take his wife back during the waiting period.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p260/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · قتادة | reports | Another reason for the warning is to prevent a child from being attributed to someone other than his father.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p260/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · قيل | reports | A woman who wanted her husband might claim menstruation after becoming clean; one who no longer wanted him could conceal menstruation until bathing and thereby forfeit his chance to return.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p260/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مجاهد، النخعي، قتادة وآخرون | reports | Baʿūla means husbands, and “that” points to the waiting period.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p260/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | A specific qualification at the end does not restrict the general opening: divorced women broadly must wait, while the right to take them back applies specifically to revocable divorces.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains the husband's degree as the dowry he paid and the money he spent on her.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261#2/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · قوم | reports | The opposing position holds the whole verse to be operative: later waiting-period verses specify the general rule rather than abrogate it.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261#2/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | prefers | Ibn al-Jawzi prefers that the verse is wholly operative: husbands may return wives only during the three-cycle waiting period, before it ends.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid explains the degree as jihad and inheritance.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو مالك | reports | Abu Malik says the husband may divorce her while she has no control over the matter.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261#2/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Zajjaj says she derives pleasure from him as he does from her, but he has a further advantage through his spending on her.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261#2/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو هريرة عن النبي | reports | Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that, if commanded to prostrate to anyone, he would command a wife to prostrate to her husband.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261#2/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابنة سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib's daughter said women addressed their husbands only as people address their governors.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261#2/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · قوم | reports | One group counts this verse among abrogated passages and identifies the waiting rule as abrogated in cases specified by other verses.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261#2/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس، الضحاك وآخرون | reports | Within the abrogation view, they say the three-cycle rule was superseded for pregnant women by 65:4 and for women divorced before consummation by 33:49. | mentions 65:4, 33:49
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261#2/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · قوم | reports | Another abrogation view says the return clause was superseded by 2:230, since a husband had formerly been entitled to return his wife even after three divorces. | mentions 2:230
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p261/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Men used to harm wives by repeatedly divorcing them once, returning as the waiting period neared its end, leaving them for a while, then divorcing again; they were forbidden this practice.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p41#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A particle is distinguished from noun and verb because its meaning is not independently intelligible; a noun is independently intelligible without indicating a specific time, whereas a verb indicates time.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p41#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The familiar definition of a particle as one whose meaning occurs in another is ambiguous: one reading would make names of accidents and attributes particles, another is plainly false, and any third needs explanation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p41#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Of the six possible combinations of noun, verb, and particle, noun+noun and noun+verb form informative sentences by agreement; the excerpt begins considering noun+particle forms.

[RAZI-FULL:v6p75/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda calls al-aqrāʾ a word of opposite meanings; the better-known analysis treats it as genuinely applying to both, like shafaq for redness and whiteness.

[RAZI-FULL:v6p76#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأخفش | reports | The gathering sense of qurʾ is supported by usage: a camel that has not gathered offspring, the womb gathering menstrual blood, a basin gathering water, stars gathering before setting, and the Qurʾān gathering letters, words, and sciences; ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm's verse is also cited.
[RAZI-FULL:v6p76#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | As a further argument for purity, Rāzī says menstrual blood does not collect in the womb but flows drop by drop; during purity it gathers in the body and accumulates toward its fullest state at the end, making the end of purity the complete qurʾ.

[RAZI-FULL:v6p76/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Rāzī says the al-Kashshāf gloss strengthens al-Shāfiʿī: divorce can occur throughout purity, so the purity period beginning after divorce must count toward the waiting period. | mentions 65:1
