[RAZI-FULL:v6p76/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although the verse's surface could suggest any three units called qurūʾ, scholars agree a woman must count three of the same kind; they disagree whether these are purity periods or menstruations.
[RAZI-FULL:v6p76/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī counts the three qurūʾ as periods of purity; Rāzī reports this also from Ibn ʿUmar, Zayd, ʿĀʾisha, the seven jurists, Mālik, Rabīʿa, and Aḥmad in one narration.
[RAZI-FULL:v6p76/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · علي وعمر وابن مسعود | reports | ʿAlī, ʿUmar, and Ibn Masʿūd count the qurūʾ as menstruations; Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī, Ibn Abī Laylā, Ibn Shubruma, and Isḥāq share this position.
[RAZI-FULL:v6p76/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Counting purity makes the waiting period shorter: the remainder of purity after divorce counts and it ends when the third menstruation begins. [RAZI-FULL:v6p76/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī argues from 65:1 that divorce is for the time when the waiting period begins; since divorce during menstruation is forbidden, the waiting period begins in purity. | mentions 65:1

[RAZI-FULL:v6p77/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī argues that either purity or menstruation can be called qurʾ, but purity is the shorter count; a woman may not be required to wait through the excess time, so menstruation is not obligatory.

[RAZI-FULL:v6p77/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المتأخرون من أصحابنا | reports | Rāzī's later colleagues answer that counting menstruations also creates a partial unit when divorce occurs during purity, but that excess is necessary because divorce during menstruation is forbidden; under the purity reading, the purity in which divorce occurs counts.
[RAZI-FULL:v6p78#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī concludes that the competing proofs weaken preference; for each person, God's ruling is what their own ijtihād leads them to.
[RAZI-FULL:v6p78#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because the end of iddah depends on menstruation or childbirth, facts men cannot directly know, the woman is trusted to report her status and her claim of ending iddah is accepted when the elapsed time permits it.

[RAZI-FULL:v6p78#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A pregnant woman who claims that she miscarried is likewise believed because she is treated as trustworthy in this matter.

ts | One interpretation includes both pregnancy and menstruation: a woman might conceal pregnancy to shorten iddah, avoid the first husband's return, marry another, or have a child attributed to the later husband.

[RAZI-FULL:v6p79/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المفسرون | reports | A second interpretation restricts the concealed matter to pregnancy: it cites 3:6, says menstruation is outside rather than created in the womb, and considers a child nobler than menstrual blood; Rāzī rejects these reasons and includes all such hidden states because they change marriage's lawful status. | mentions 3:6

[RAZI-FULL:v6p79/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | One analysis takes buʿūla as a plural of baʿl, like other collective plurals; the feminine ending reinforces the group's feminine form and is permitted only in established Arabic usage, not with every noun.

[RAZI-FULL:v6p81#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One reading of men's degree lists advantages in intellect, blood money, inheritance, leadership and legal roles, polygyny and concubinage, unilateral divorce and revocation, and a larger share of booty; Rāzī says these leave women vulnerable and make men more bound to fulfill their rights, since greater blessings make abuse more culpable.

laim of revocation after the waiting period, her statement prevails even if her master calls her a liar, according to al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr, and al-Nuʿman.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#10/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · يعقوب | reports | Yaqub and Muhammad say the master’s claim prevails in a dispute over a slave wife’s revocation and that the master has the stronger claim to her.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#10/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The word “return” implies that the marital bond was removed; al-Qurtubi’s school says intercourse is forbidden to the revocably divorced woman, so return restores permissibility.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#10/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الليث بن سعد | reports | Al-Layth, Abu Hanifa, and their followers say marital rulings remain intact and divorce only reduces the allotted number; revocation turns the wife back from the path toward separation as the waiting period expires, a figurative return.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#10/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | Al-Qurtubi distinguishes his school’s literal return: intercourse has actually become forbidden, so revocation restores a real, presently lost permission.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#10/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | “More entitled” is used when two rights compete and one prevails: the husband’s right during the waiting period exceeds her right to herself, which begins only after it ends.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#10/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله | reports | The author compares the phrasing to the Prophetic statement that a previously married woman is more entitled to herself than her guardian.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The verse comprehensively includes all rights within marriage.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbi interprets the degree as the bridal payment.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | Another reported interpretation takes the degree to mean the permissibility of disciplining a wife.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | In sum, the degree indicates preference and that the husband’s right over his wife is more binding than hers over him.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Scholars explain Ibn Abbas’s self-adornment as matching one’s appearance to age, time, and suitability: a trimmed mustache can suit an older man but look poor on a young man without a full beard.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet said that God commanded him to let his beard grow and trim his mustache.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Men’s adornment also includes suitable clothing and, depending on the individual, kohl; perfume, tooth-cleaning, grooming, purification, and nail-clipping suit everyone, with henna for older men and rings for men of all ages.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | A husband should adorn himself in a fitting way to please his wife and help preserve her chastity, and attend to her sexual needs; if unable to fulfill her in bed, he should take medicines that increase potency and desire.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Daraja means rank or status; the author also connects its root to a road’s edge, traversing one’s lifetime, stairs, and strength-related words such as rajul and rajīl.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The man’s additional degree lies in intellect, strength, financial support, blood money, inheritance, and jihad.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · حميد | rejects | Humayd is reported to interpret the degree as the beard; al-Qurtubi says this, if correctly attributed, is weak and unsupported by the wording or meaning.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#11/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن العربي | reports | Ibn al-Arabi claims men’s superiority is clear, citing woman’s creation from man and the husband’s authority over her actions, fasting, and pilgrimage.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#12/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet said that if he were to command anyone to prostrate to another besides God, he would command a wife to prostrate to her husband.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#12/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reads the degree as an exhortation for men to show good companionship and generosity toward women; Ibn Atiyya calls this a fine and excellent interpretation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#12/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الماوردي | reports | Al-Mawardi suggests the degree concerns marital rights: the husband can end the marriage, whereas the wife cannot, and she must answer his call to bed though he is not likewise obliged.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#12/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet warned that angels curse a woman who refuses her husband’s call to bed until morning.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#12/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Aziz means that God’s sovereignty is invincible and unchallenged; al-Hakim means He knows and acts rightly.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#2/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشاعر | reports | A cited poem about the winds blowing at their appointed season illustrates qarʾ as a time.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#2/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الأعشى | reports | Al-Aʿsha's poem uses quruʾ for women's periods of purity.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#2/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · شاعر | reports | Another poet describes a stabbed man with blood like a menstruating woman's, using quruʾ for menstruation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#2/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قوم | reports | Some derive qarʾ from water gathered in a basin and connect Qurʾan with gathering meanings or letters; they also cite a camel that has not gathered a fetus.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#2/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عمر بن عبد البر | rejects | Ibn Abd al-Barr rejects deriving qarʾ from gathering water because qarʾ is hamzated whereas the water word is not; al-Qurtubi agrees, following lexicographers who name the water qurā.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#2/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قوم | reports | Another view defines qarʾ as transition from purity to menstruation or from menstruation to purity; one Shafiʿi position counts only the transition from purity into menstruation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#2/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | If qarʾ means transition, the word could cover three cycles across both states; al-Qurtubi reasons that the verse does not count transition from menstruation to purity, leaving three transitions beginning with the purity in which divorce occurred.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#2/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Because a Sunnah divorce occurs during purity, the first counted transition begins with that purity; this yields three complete quruʾ without resort to metaphor.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الكيا الطبري | reports | Al-Kiya al-Tabari calls the transition analysis a strong argument for al-Shafiʿi and adds that purity-to-menstruation signals an unpregnant womb, since pregnant women usually do not menstruate.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الزهري | reports | Al-Zuhri says that a woman divorced partway through a purity discards what remains and then counts three full periods of purity.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عمر | reports | Ibn Abd al-Barr knows no other proponent of the purity view besides Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri who discards the remaining purity; on that view release comes only upon entering the fourth menstruation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن القاسم ومالك وجمهور أصحابه والشافعي وعلماء المدينة | reports | Ibn al-Qasim, Malik and most of his associates, al-Shafiʿi, and Medina's scholars say the marriage bond ends at the first spot of blood of the third menstruation; Zayd, Aisha, Ibn Umar, Ahmad, and Dawud also held this.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الكيا الطبري | reports | Al-Kiya says menstruation-to-purity differs because conception can occur after menstruation and pregnancy may later stop bleeding; Arab praise for pregnancy in purity is illustrated by a poem recited by Aisha.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Linguists say a woman may have qaraʾ when she menstruates or becomes pure, and also use the verb for pregnancy; they agree qarʾ means a time, leaving the counted unit ambiguous here.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Qurtubi seeks the counted unit in 65:1: divorce is commanded at a time that counts toward the waiting period, and the following command is to count that period. | mentions 65:1
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet told Umar to have the divorcer take his wife back and keep her until she is pure, menstruates, and becomes pure again, then said that is the waiting period for which women are to be divorced; al-Qurtubi treats this as explicit evidence that purity counts. | mentions 65:1
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | A divorce during menstruation does not count that period, while most jurists count the purity in which divorce occurs; this makes the purity interpretation stronger.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو بكر بن عبد الرحمن | reports | Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman says every jurist they encountered held Aisha's view that quruʾ are periods of purity.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | On the majority purity view, divorce in an unconsummated pure period counts even the remaining moment; after two more periods of purity, the woman leaves the bond when the third menstruation begins.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#3/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو بكر بن عبد الرحمن | reports | A divorce during a purity in which intercourse occurred is valid but sinful, and the woman counts the remainder of that purity.

:2:228#4/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | rejects | The Prophet’s permission to divorce during any part of a nonconsummated purity, without specifying its beginning or end, is evidence against al-Zuhri’s timing restriction.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#4/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa agrees that a woman divorced while menstruating does not count that menstruation or the following purity, but begins with the menstruation after that purity; al-Qurtubi instead counts the purity.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#4/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Arabic may use a plural time expression for a partial total: 2:197 calls the pilgrimage months, though the period is two months and part of a third, so three quruʾ can likewise include partial units. | mentions 2:197
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#4/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أشهب | reports | Ashhab says the marital bond and inheritance continue until the blood is confirmed as menstruation, so a nonmenstrual discharge is not mistaken for it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#4/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله | reports | The Kufans cite the Prophet’s instruction to Fatima bint Abi Hubaysh: treat the bleeding as a vein, stop praying at menstruation, then purify and pray between periods.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#4/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans infer from 65:4, which names menstruation as what women may despair of and assigns months in its absence, that menstruation is the waiting-period measure. | mentions 65:4
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#4/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عمر | reports | Umar said before the Companions that a slave woman’s waiting period is two menstruations, half the free woman’s; he would have made it one and a half if possible.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#4/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Because no Companion objected to Umar, al-Qurtubi treats his ruling as consensus, supported by ten Companions including the four caliphs.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#4/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | Al-Qurtubi reads the three quruʾ as three complete menstrual periods: a purity-based count could include the remainder of the purity in which divorce occurred, then only part of another.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#4/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | On his view, a woman divorced during an unconsummated purity starts at the next menstruation, counts three periods, and leaves the waiting period after bathing from the third.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#4/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | He invokes the grammatical gender of quruʾ alongside masculine ayyām in 69:7 as a response in the debate over the intended sense of quruʾ. | mentions 69:7
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The phrase in 2:197, “pilgrimage months,” refers to two months and part of a third, illustrating plural wording for a partial amount. | mentions 2:197
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله | reports | The majority cite a report from Aisha that the divorce allotment for a slave woman is two and her quruʾ are two menstruations; al-Qurtubi notes that Mazahir ibn Aslam alone transmitted it and is weak.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar is reported to have said that whichever spouse is enslaved reduces the divorce allotment; a group of scholars followed him.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عكرمة | reports | Ikrima, al-Zuhri, and al-Nakhaʿi interpret what is in the wombs as menstruation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عمر | reports | Umar and Ibn Abbas interpret what is in the wombs as pregnancy.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r14] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the phrase includes both menstruation and pregnancy, on the premise that a pregnant woman can menstruate.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r15] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Because only women know their menstruation or purity and the waiting period depends on it, their statement about its ending or continuation is accepted and they are entrusted with disclosure.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r16] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سليمان بن يسار | reports | Sulayman ibn Yasar says people were not ordered to inspect women’s private parts; the matter was entrusted to women as persons trusted to report it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r17] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The ban on concealment protects the husband: falsely claiming menstruation removes his revocation right; falsely denying it can impose extra maintenance or prevent revocation until the term expires; concealing pregnancy can likewise block his right.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Among scholars who take quruʾ as menstruations, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Tawus, Ibn Shubruma, and al-Awzaʿi say the waiting period ends after bathing from the third period, when revocation also ends.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · شريك | reports | Sharik says that even if a woman delays bathing for twenty years, her husband retains the right of revocation until she bathes.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · إسحاق بن راهويه | reports | Ishaq ibn Rahawayh says that entering the third menstruation ends the marriage bond and revocation right, though she may not marry until bathing from it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | A similar position is attributed to Ibn Abbas, but al-Qurtubi calls it weak and counters it with 2:234, where reaching the term precedes freedom to act about oneself. | mentions 2:234
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafiʿi counts the transition from purity into menstruation as a quruʾ, shortening the waiting period: a divorce at the very end of purity is counted at once, and transition into the third ends the bond.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الجمهور | reports | The majority of scholars hold that a menstruating slave woman waits two menstrual periods after divorce.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن سيرين | reports | Ibn Sirin says he would regard a slave woman’s waiting period as the same as a free woman’s unless a Prophetic practice established otherwise, since the practice deserves following.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#5/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الأصم عبد الرحمن بن كيسان وداود بن علي | reports | Al-Asamm Abd al-Rahman ibn Kaysan, Dawud ibn Ali, and other literalists say the waiting-period verses apply equally to slave and free women.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says the verse was revealed because women in pre-Islamic times concealed pregnancy so they could attribute the child to a new husband.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The conditional is a severe warning that reinforces the ban on concealment and the duty to state truthfully what is in the womb.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The conditional does not imply that unbelievers may conceal; like “if you are my brother, do not wrong me,” it means faith should keep a person from such conduct.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Baʿūla is the plural of baʿl, “husband”; he is so called for his elevation over the wife through the marital rights he possesses.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رجل من أشجع | reports | A man from Ashjaʿ told the Prophet he feared his divorced pregnant wife might remarry and the child be attributed to another man; the verse was revealed and the Ashjaʿi woman returned to him.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن المنذر | reports | Ibn al-Mundhir says the scholars known to him reject a claim of three periods and completed waiting period within ten days, unless the woman says she miscarried a fetus with discernible form.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Malik accepts a claim of completed waiting period when the stated duration is one in which it could normally end; if the duration is exceptionally rare, he reports two opinions.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | In the Mudawwana, Malik accepts a claim of three periods in a month if women confirm it; Shurayh agrees, and Ali praised Shurayh’s judgment.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Ali told Shurayh “qālūn,” meaning he had judged correctly and well, on accepting a woman’s claim when other women corroborated it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · محمد | reports | In Muhammad’s book, the woman is not believed to have completed the three periods in less than a month and a half.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو ثور | reports | Abu Thawr sets the minimum at forty-seven days, reasoning from a minimum purity of fifteen days and a minimum menstruation of one day.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#6/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النعمان | reports | Al-Nuʿman and al-Shafiʿi do not believe a claim of completed waiting period in less than sixty days.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#7/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The word baʿl also means lord because of elevation in lordship, as in 37:125, where it refers to a deity addressed as lord. | mentions 37:125
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#7/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن المنذر | reports | Ibn al-Mundhir says the Qurʾanic evidence cited together with scholarly consensus suffices, without recounting earlier reports on the subject.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#7/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Malik counts intercourse during the waiting period as revocation when he intends to return her, even without witnesses; the wife should prevent intercourse until he witnesses, and Ishaq agrees.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#7/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Baʿl has the plural baʿūla like dhakar/dhukūra and faḥl/fuḥūla; the group feminine ending is emphatic and irregular, so its use is attested rather than extended by analogy,

 though it may instead be a feminine ending on faʿūl.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#7/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Baʿūla can also be a verbal noun; baʿala means to become a husband, while mubāʿala and biʿāl mean intercourse, and a man is his wife’s baʿl while she is his baʿla.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#7/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet described the days of Tashriq as days of eating, drinking, and intercourse.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#7/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Baʿl can also mean the owner or master of something.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#7/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Here “returning them” means taking them back in revocation; he distinguishes revocation during the waiting period, linked to Ibn Umar, from return after it, linked to Maʿqil.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#7/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The general waiting-period clause covers all divorced women, including those divorced three times and those divorced fewer; the right of husbands to revoke is specifically for the latter.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#7/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | There is consensus that a free husband may revoke a consummated wife after one or two divorces during her waiting period even against her will; after it expires, she is independent and can return only through a new proposal and marriage with guardian and witnesses.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#7/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · المهلب | reports | Al-Muhallab says revocation during the waiting period requires no marriage formalities beyond witnesses to the revocation, a consensus he links to 65:2, which mentions witnesses for revocation but not for marriage or divorce. | mentions 65:2
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#8/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رسول الله | reports | Malik’s intention-based rule cites the Prophetic report that deeds are judged by intentions and each person receives according to what he intended.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#8/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | When intercourse occurs without intending revocation, Malik says the husband may revoke during the waiting period but must not have intercourse again until she has completed an interval to establish that his unlawful semen is cleared.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#8/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن القاسم | reports | Ibn al-Qasim says that after the waiting period she cannot marry her former husband or another man during the remaining clearance period; a marriage then is annulled, but does not create permanent prohibition because the semen was his.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#8/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Sirin, al-Zuhri, Ata, Tawus, and al-Thawri hold that intercourse itself is revocation; witnesses should be used, as held also by the Hanafi school, al-Awzaʿi, and Ibn Abi Layla.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#8/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عمر | reports | Abu Umar reports a view among some Maliki authorities that intercourse revokes in every case, whether intended or not; al-Layth adopted it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#8/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Scholars agree that a seller with an option to cancel a slave-girl sale can have intercourse during the option period, thereby reclaiming her and undoing the sale; the author says a revocable wife has the same status.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#8/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | A kiss or other intimate touch with intent to revoke counts as revocation; without that intent, kissing or touching is sinful but does not constitute revocation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The Sunnah is to witness revocation before intercourse, kissing, or intimate touching.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa and his companions agree that the revocable wife may adorn herself for her husband with perfume, jewelry, and dress.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab says she should ask permission, may wear clothes and jewelry, and if they share one house they should separate with a curtain; Qatada also recommends announcing entry with a greeting and throat-clearing.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafiʿi treats a revocably divorced wife as forbidden to her former husband like an irrevocably divorced woman until he revokes, and holds that revocation requires spoken words.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa, his companions, and al-Thawri count intercourse, lustful touching, or looking at her private parts with desire as revocation; they recommend witnesses.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Malik, al-Shafiʿi, Ishaq, Abu Ubayd, and Abu Thawr say these acts do not constitute revocation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · القاضي أبو محمد | reports | Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad says revocation is valid by intercourse, a kiss, and all other forms of sexual enjoyment, while speech-based revocation is undisputed.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن المواز | reports | Ibn al-Mawwaz includes pleasurable touching and looking at her private parts or nearby beauty when done intending revocation; this differs from al-Shafiʿi’s speech-only rule, also attributed to Abu Thawr, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Abu Qilaba.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Malik and al-Shafiʿi do not allow the husband to travel with a revocable wife until he revokes; Abu Hanifa and his companions allow travel before revocation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · زفر | reports | Reports from Zufar differ: al-Hasan ibn Ziyad transmits permission to travel before revocation, while Amr ibn Khalid transmits that travel must wait until revocation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Malik says he must not be alone with her or enter without permission; she remains covered, he may not see her hair, they may eat together if someone else is present, but not sleep together in one room.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228#9/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن القاسم | reports | Ibn al-Qasim says Malik later retracted the permission to enter, maintaining that the husband may not enter or see her hair.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | After discussing the oath of abstention and the possibility of divorce, God explains the divorced woman's status.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قوم | reports | Another grammatical explanation supplies an omitted lām, making the phrase mean let them wait.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · جمهور الناس | reports | The majority read quruʾ on the fuʿūl pattern with final hamza.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · نافع | reports | A reading reported from Nafi has quru with a doubled, kasra-bearing wāw and no hamza.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan reads qarʾ with fatḥa on qāf, a silent rāʾ, and tanwīn.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r14] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Asmaʿi says quruʾ is the plural of aqruʾ and aqraʾ, with singular qarʾ on ḍamma-bearing qāf.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r15] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو زيد | reports | Abu Zayd gives qarʾ with fatḥa and says a woman is muqriʾ when she menstruates; forms also describe her becoming pure.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r16] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash says the verb can describe a woman becoming one who menstruates and gives a form for saying she menstruated once or twice.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r17] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قوم | reports | Lexical explanations include the cessation of menstruation, the interval between two periods, and a due time approaching, according to al-Jawhari.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r18] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abu Amr ibn al-Ala says some Arabs use quruʾ for menstruation, some for purity, and some for the combined period of purity with menstruation; al-Nahhas transmits this.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r19] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أهل الكوفة | reports | The Kufan jurists take the three quruʾ as menstrual periods, a view attributed to Umar, Ali, Ibn Masud, Abu Musa, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Ikrima, and al-Suddi.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that a husband once retained the right to take back his wife after divorce, even after three divorces; this was abrogated by 2:229, Divorce is twice. | mentions 2:229
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r20] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أهل الحجاز | reports | The Hijazi jurists take the three quruʾ as periods of purity, a view attributed to Aisha, Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Zuhri, Aban ibn Uthman, and al-Shafiʿi.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r21] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Each school explains quruʾ through gathering: blood gathers in the womb during menstruation or in the body during purity.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r22] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Qurtubi identifies the underlying sense of qarʾ as a time or appointed interval, as in a wind blowing at its season, and introduces poetry as evidence.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Although general in wording, the verse concerns divorced women whose marriages were consummated; women divorced before consummation are excluded by 33:49, and pregnant women by 65:4. | mentions 33:49, 65:4
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The purpose of the quruʾ period is to establish whether the womb is clear, unlike a widow's waiting period, which is an act of worship.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The waiting period for a young girl who has not menstruated and an older woman who has despaired of menstruation is counted in months, as explained later.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قوم | reports | Some say the general wording originally i

ncluded girls and older women and they were later excluded; al-Qurtubi calls this weak and says the verse addresses menstruating women, the usual case.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Yatarabbaṣna means they wait, as previously explained.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أهل اللسان | reports | Linguists take the indicative statement as an imperative, like the command that mothers nurse their children; Ibn al-Shajari cites usage examples and says this is the consensus of speakers of Arabic. | mentions 2:233
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:228/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن العربي | rejects | Ibn al-Arabi rejects the imperative analysis: the verse reports a legal rule, so a divorced woman who does not wait is outside the law, not proof that God's report is false.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The divorced women meant are those whose marriages were consummated and who menstruate; verses and reports show that other categories have different rules.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r10] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In the report about Ibn ʿUmar, the Prophet ordered him to take his wife back, wait through purity, menstruation, then purity, and only then retain or divorce her before intercourse; this is the prescribed waiting period.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r11] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Although the expected plural for three is the paucity form aqruʾ, Arabic freely uses either plural pattern in place of the other; broad coverage of divorced women may also suit the abundance form.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r12] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | They must not conceal a child or menstruation to shorten the waiting period and nullify the husband’s right of revocation; doing so is incompatible with faith.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r13] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Buʿūl means the husbands of the divorced women.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r14] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Husbands have the stronger right to restore their wives to marriage by revocation during the waiting period, when the divorce is revocable as the next verse specifies.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r15] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The pronoun refers more narrowly than its antecedent, which is permissible as if the explicit noun had been repeated and restricted.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r16] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Baʿūla is the plural of baʿl, with tāʾ marking a collective plural like ʿumūma and khuʾūla; it may instead be a verbal noun used adjectivally or stand for omitted “people of their husbands.”
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r17] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Afʿal here has the sense of an active participle.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r18] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | “During that” means during the waiting period.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r19] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Seeking reconciliation is not a condition for a valid revocation; the phrase urges reconciliation and bars intending harm to the woman.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Although phrased as a statement, “they wait” functions as a command; this wording stresses its binding force and prompt compliance, while the initial predicate construction adds emphasis.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r20] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Women have rights against men corresponding in obligation and enforceability to the duties they owe, though the rights are not of the same kind.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r21] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The men’s degree may be an additional right and advantage, since their rights concern themselves while women’s include dower, maintenance, and freedom from harm.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r22] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Alternatively, the degree is honor and merit: men maintain and care for women and share marriage’s purpose, while being specially charged with care and spending.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r23] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | God is mighty to punish those who violate these rulings and wise in legislating them for purposes and benefits.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The wording stirs women to wait: because their souls incline toward men, they must restrain them and make them wait.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The three qurūʾ are an accusative of time or a direct object: women wait for their passage.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Qurūʾ can mean menstrual periods, as in the Prophetic instruction to stop praying during them, or the intervals of purity, as in al-Aʿshā’s verse.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | prefers | The word originally denotes transition from purity to menstruation; Bayḍāwī prefers purity here because it indicates the womb is clear.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · الحنفية | reports | The Ḥanafīs take qurūʾ here as periods of purity, which indicate the womb’s being clear.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The command “divorce them for their waiting period” supports purity as the intended sense, since lawful divorce does not occur during menstruation. | mentions 65:1
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:228/r9] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | holds | The report “a slave woman’s divorce is two divorces and her waiting period is two menstruations” does not outweigh the rigorously transmitted Ibn ʿUmar report.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p109#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The divorced women intended are those with whom the marriage was consummated and who menstruate.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p109#2/r10] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | prefers | On al-Nasafī’s view, divorce at the end of menstruation does not count toward the waiting period, whereas al-Shāfiʿī counts divorce at the end of purity; three is a fixed number, not fewer.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p109#2/r11] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Thalāthata is either a direct object, ‘wait for three qurūʾ to pass,’ or an adverbial of duration, ‘wait for a period of three qurūʾ.’
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p109#2/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The declarative form means a command; it strengthens the order by presenting compliance as already occurring, like a prayer phrased as a confident report of fulfillment.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p109#2/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The nominal sentence adds emphasis by suggesting permanence, while mention of their own selves stirs women to master desire and wait.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p109#2/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | prefers | Qurūʾ means menstruations, supported by reports directing women to leave prayer during their periods and setting a slave woman’s waiting period at two menstruations.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p109#2/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · النبي | reports | The Prophet says to leave prayer during the days of one’s periods; al-Nasafī cites this as evidence that qurūʾ means menstruation. No grading is stated.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p109#2/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · النبي | reports | A Prophetic report says a slave woman’s divorce is two and her waiting period is two menstruations; this supports the menstrual sense. No grading is stated.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p109#2/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The waiting months for women who no longer menstruate in 65:4 replace menstruations, not intervals of purity, supporting his reading of qurūʾ as menses. | mentions 6, 5, :, 4
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p109#2/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | prefers | The purpose of waiting is to establish that the womb is empty, which menstruation reveals; an enslaved woman’s waiting is likewise measured by a menstruation.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p109#2/r9] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · الشافعي | rejects | Al-Shāfiʿī reads qurūʾ as intervals of purity; al-Nasafī argues that this can end the waiting period at two periods and part of the third, so the prescribed three are not completed.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The plural of abundance qurūʾ replaces the plural of paucity aqruʾ because the forms overlap in collectivity and qurūʾ was more commonly used.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r10] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Equality concerns the comparable goodness of obligations, not identical tasks: if she washes or bakes for him, he need not do the same, but reciprocates suitably as a man.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r11] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | The men’s degree may be their additional right and merit in managing her affairs, or their maintenance and control of the marriage bond.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r12] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | God is mighty, beyond challenge in His affairs, and wise, commanding only what is right and good.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | What they might conceal is a child, menstrual blood, or both: a woman seeking separation could hide pregnancy to avoid delayed divorce or her husband relenting, or hide menstruation and falsely claim purity to hasten divorce.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Invoking belief in God and the Last Day magnifies the warning: one who believes in God and His punishment would not dare such grave acts.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Buʿūla is the plural of baʿl, with the feminine tāʾ marking the plural.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Their husbands are more entitled to take them back; calling them husbands after divorce shows that a revocable divorce does not itself prohibit intercourse.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | ‘Within that’ means during the waiting period.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | If the husband seeks reconciliation and the wife refuses, his decision prevails; she has no independent right to refuse the return.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The husband’
<<part 19 ends; continues in part 20>>

s superior right applies when he seeks reconciliation and kindness, not harm to his wife.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p110/r9] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Women have duties corresponding in goodness to their rights, in a manner recognized by religious law and custom; neither spouse may impose what is not owed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p437/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The word rajul is linked to strength: the strongest man is arjal, a strong horse is rajīl, and the leg is named for its power in walking.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p437/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The author cites a copied couplet from Abū Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr as evidence for the word al-rajula, referring to a woman’s honor.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p437/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Daraja means rank or station; its root evokes folding something away and the stages by which people disappear, so a degree is a step in ascent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p437/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Qurʾ originally denotes a regularly recurring time; the source applies it to a star’s rising or setting and says the verb can mean either.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p437/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عمرو، يونس، أبو عبيد | reports | These authorities say a woman’s qurʾ can mean either her menstruation or her purity, making the word one of opposites.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p437/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Some Arabs use one qurʾ for the combined period of menstruation and purity; others mean the interval between two menstruations.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p437/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash says aqraʾat means she became a menstruating woman, while qarʾat without the hamza form means that she menstruated.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p437/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | One derivation makes qurʾ mean gathering: menstruation gathers blood in the womb, while purity gathers it in the body.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p437/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Raḥim means the female genital opening and is also used metaphorically for kinship, as in maintaining family ties.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p437/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Baʿl means husband; baʿala can mean becoming a husband, and bāʿala describes intercourse between spouses and their mutual conduct.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p437/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Baʿl can also mean a king or lord, the self-sufficient idol, or a date palm; its plurals are buʿūl and buʿūla, with a nonproductive feminine collective tāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p452/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Some reported occasions for this verse do not qualify as occasions; its placement is clear because divorce follows the bounded abstention of ila and then requires a three-cycle waiting period.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p452/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Another analysis deletes an implied noun and أن to make the clause a predicate; Abu Hayyan considers this construction very remote.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p452/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The verse's general term is restricted to divorced women who had intercourse and have menstrual cycles; unconsummated, pregnant, and postmenopausal women have different rulings stated elsewhere.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p452/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس، وقتادة | reports | Ibn Abbas and Qatada say the ruling initially covered all divorced women and was then abrogated for all except consummated women with menstrual cycles.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p452/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abu Hayyan calls that abrogation account weak: a general expression used for a specific class is common and needs no separate proof of abrogation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p452/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari treats the wording as an absolute term that can refer to all or some members of a class, like a homonym.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p452/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abu Hayyan rejects that account: a general term denotes each individual and is not an absolute term covering a whole or part at choice.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p452/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A general term has one semantic assignment covering every individual, unlike a homonym, which has distinct assignments for its separate meanings.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p452/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Syntactically, al-muṭallaqāt is the subject and yataربbaṣna its predicate; formally declarative, the clause conveys a command.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p452/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufan analysis takes it as a command in both form and meaning, with an omitted lām: ليتربصن.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p453/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari says casting a command as a statement intensifies it and urges immediate compliance, as though the women had already obeyed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p453/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | He compares this declarative form to a prayer for mercy stated as a fact, expressing confidence that the prayer will be answered.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p453/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Abu Hayyan approves the emphasis account and says the nominal clause strengthens it by naming the subject twice, explicitly and through its pronoun.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p453/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | A cited rhetorical account says fronting a subject can claim that an action is exclusive to it, as in claiming to be the sole writer to the sultan.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p453/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The same account says fronting may instead emphasize an established trait without implying exclusivity, as in saying that someone gives generously.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p453/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Yataربbaṣna means that divorced women wait and do not proceed to marry.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p453/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · القرطبي | reports | Al-Qurtubi takes the statement as a literal report of the law: a divorced woman who does not wait is not following the law.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p453/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | The declarative analysis is preferable because what is reported must occur, whereas commands may or may not be obeyed, and waiting requires no intention.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p453/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Tarabbaṣa is transitive in meaning; the object is omitted here but appears explicitly in Quranic examples about waiting for outcomes and the passage of time. | mentions 9:52, 52:30
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p454#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأوزاعي، والثوري، والحسن بن صالح، ومالك، والشافعي | reports | Al-Awzai, al-Thawri, Hasan b. Salih, Malik, and al-Shafii identify qurūʾ as purity periods.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p454#2/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مالك، والشافعي، وأحمد، وداود | reports | They count the remainder of the purity in which divorce occurred, even if only an hour, then two later purity periods; the waiting period ends at the first sign of the third menstruation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p454#2/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أشهب | reports | Ashhab says marital bonds and inheritance do not end until the blood is confirmed as menstruation, since it might be an isolated non-menstrual discharge.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p454#2/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن شهاب | reports | Ibn Shihab unusually excludes the remaining purity at divorce, requiring three full qurūʾ and ending the waiting period only when the fourth menstruation begins.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p454#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مالك | reports | Zayd b. Thabit, Ubada b. al-Samit, Abu al-Darda, Aisha, Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, al-Zuhri, Aban b. Uthman, Sulayman b. Yasar, al-Awzai, al-Thawri, Hasan b. Salih, Malik, al-Shafii and Hijazi jurists identify qurūʾ as periods of purity.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p454#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أحمد | reports | Ahmad says he formerly held that qurʾ meant purity but now adopts the view that it means menstruation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p454#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الشافعي | reports | A report from al-Shafii defines a qurʾ as the transition from purity into menstruation, not the transition from menstruation to purity.

item.text: The later sources add legal subquestions about revocation: whether intimacy is allowed before it, what acts count as revocation, whether witnesses are needed, and how a woman’s account of her waiting period is assessed. I’ll keep these questions separate from the dispute over the meaning of *qurūʾ*.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p461/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · زيد بن أسلم، وابنه | reports | Zayd ibn Aslam and his son identify the degree as the wife's duty to obey her husband, while he is not bound to obey her.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p461/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbi locates the degree in the dowry, the husband's right to liʿān if he accuses her, and her punishment if she accuses him.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p461/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Ishaq says the degree is the husband's responsibility to maintain and otherwise care for her, although both share sexual enjoyment.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p461/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قتادة، وابن زيد | reports | Qatada and Ibn Zayd explain the degree as the husband's control of the marital bond and his possession of divorce.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p462/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The exegetes' summary indicates that men's degree over women entails preference.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p462/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “A degree” is an indefinite subject, “for men” its predicate, and “over them” attaches to the predicate's implied state.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p462/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Alternatively, “over them” may be a circumstantial phrase describing the indefinite “degree,” attached to an omitted governor.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p462/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | It is invalid to make “over them” the predicate and “for men” a circumstantial phrase, because its semantic governor cannot precede both sentence parts.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p462/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو الحسن | reports | Abu al-Hasan allows a circumstantial phrase between subject and predicate; other grammarians prohibit it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p462/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Might and wisdom close the verse because it contains command, prohibition, permission, and obligation; dominance and wise ordering suit these legal duties.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | For numerals three through ten, the counted noun normally takes a paucity plural; since aqraʾ exists, the use of the abundance plural qurūʾ needs explanation.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الأخفش | reports | A woman’s qarʾ can denote her time of menstruation or purity; al-Akhfash distinguishes aqraʾat, becoming menstruating, from qaraʾat, menstruating.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Other definitions are menstruation together with purity, or the interval between two menstruations.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Qarʾ may originally mean gathering, as in gathering water in a basin and reciting the Qurʾān.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | One explanation counts all the divorced women together: each waits three periods, making the aggregate number of periods large.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Another explanation allows one plural pattern to stand broadly in place of the other.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A third explanation derives qurūʾ from qarʾ with fatḥa; aqraʾ would be irregular because afʿāl is not a regular plural for this faʿl pattern.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · المبرد | reports | Al-Mubarrad estimates “three of periods,” with min omitted; Abu al-Baqāʾ's expanded estimate is the same analysis.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | One proposed root sense is a recurring appointed time: the star's qarʾ is its rising or setting, and aqraʾa al-najm means it rose or set.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشاعر | reports | An unnamed poet uses qāriʾ for the appointed time when winds blow, supporting the time sense.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Other proposed origins are transition from purity to menstruation or the reverse, and gathering; the gathering-water etymology is rejected because that verb has a weak y-root while qarʾ is hamzated.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#2/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Linguists disagree whether menstruation and purity are homonyms or share an underlying common meaning such as gathering, time, or transition.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · عمرو بن كلثوم | reports | Ibn Kulthūm's verse uses taqraʾ for gathering a fetus; on the gathering derivation, menstruation gathers blood in the womb and purity gathers blood in the body.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · جمهور أهل اللسان | reports | Most linguists, including Abū ʿAmr, Yūnus, and Abū ʿUbayda, take menstruation and purity as homonyms/opposites rather than senses sharing one meaning.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الأعشى | reports | Al-Aʿshā uses qurūʾ for periods of purity, as the context refers to the loss of the women's pure intervals.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشاعر | reports | An unnamed poet uses qurūʾ for menstruation, likening a man's flowing blood to a menstruating woman's blood.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Aṣmaʿī transmits qarʾ with ḍamma, while Abū Zayd transmits it with fatḥa; both forms mean the same.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan reads thalāthata qarū, with fatḥa on qāf, silent rāʾ, light wāw, and no hamza; he treats the number as annexed to a generic noun and uses a dialect form of qarʾ.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#3/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزهري | reports | Al-Zuhrī, also reported from Nāfiʿ, reads qurūww with doubled wāw, easing the hamza to wāw and assimilating the preceding wāw.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The lām in lahunna is attached to yaḥillu and is the lām of communication, as in “I said to you.”
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The stronger parsing makes mā a relative pronoun meaning “that which”; its resumptive pronoun is omitted, estimated mā khalaqahu.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternatively, mā is an indefinite noun described by the following clause; like the relative analysis, it has an omitted resumptive pronoun.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Mā may refer to the fetus, treated grammatically as nonrational, or to menstrual blood.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#4/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Fī arḥāmihinna can attach directly to khalaqa, or modify the omitted resumptive pronoun circumstantially: what God created, existing in their wombs.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#4/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abū al-Baqāʾ calls the circumstantial reading prospective, since at the time of creation the fetus is not yet a thing until its creation is complete.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#4/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · مبشر بن عبيد | reports | Mubashshir ibn ʿUbayd reads both hāʾ pronouns with ḍamma, the original form and a Hijazi usage; kasra harmonizes with a preceding yāʾ or kasra.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#5/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The conditional's answer may be omitted and recovered from the preceding prohibition: if they believe, they must not conceal.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#5/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans and Abū Zayd allow the answer to precede the conditional, with the earlier prohibition serving as its answer.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#5/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | Taking in as meaning idh, “when,” is a weak analysis.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#5/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · مسلمة بن محارب | reports | The majority pronounce the tāʾ of baʿūlatuhunna with fatḥa; Muslimah ibn Muḥārib silences it to avoid consecutive vowel movements, as in a reading of 43:30. | mentions 43:30
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#5/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd reports silencing the nominative ending in rusulunā; Abū ʿAmr reports that Tamīm similarly silences nominatives such as yaʿlamuhum. | mentions 43:30
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#5/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Aḥaqqu is the predicate of baʿūlatuhunna and means “entitled,” not comparative: outsiders have no claim, and a wife's refusal does not invalidate a husband's revocation.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#5/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Baʿūla is the plural of baʿl, husband; its tāʾ marks a feminine collective plural like fuhūla and dhukūra, a pattern that is not productive.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#5/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Baʿūla is also a verbal noun of baʿala; ḥasanat al-tabāʿul describes a good wife, while bāʿalahā is a euphemism for intercourse.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#6/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Bi-raddihinna is attached to aḥaqqu.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#6/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | If fī dhālika attaches to aḥaqqu, dhālika means the waiting period: the husband has the right to revoke during it, restoring her to the marriage.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#6/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Alternatively, fī dhālika attaches to the act of revocation, and dhālika refers to marriage.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#6/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The pronoun in baʿūlatuhunna refers to some divorced women, specifically those whose divorces are revocable.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#6/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | prefers | The Shaykh prefers an understood annexed noun, “husbands of their revocably divorced women,” which makes the pronoun refer to all divorced women.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#6/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The clause has a fronted predicate; its balanced ellipsis removes “against their husbands” where “against them” appears, and “for their husbands” where “for them” appears.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#7/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 ·

author | reports | Bi-l-maʿrūf can attach to the predicate governing lahunna, meaning their due is established according to recognized practice.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#7/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternatively, it modifies mithl as a deleted adjective; because mithl does not become definite through annexation, the phrase is nominative in this parse rather than accusative in the first.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#7/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The stronger parse makes li-l-rijāli a fronted predicate and darajatun the delayed subject; ʿalayhinna either attaches to that predicate or is a fronted circumstantial modifier of daraja.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#7/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abū al-Baqāʾ allows ʿalayhinna as predicate and li-l-rijāli as a circumstantial modifier, arguing that preposing a prepositional phrase before a semantic governor can be strong.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228#7/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | rejects | The Shaykh rejects this parse outright: the circumstantial precedes both sentence constituents, unlike the disputed intermediate order; Abū al-Ḥasan allows the latter, while others forbid it.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Al-muṭallaqātu is a subject with yatarabbaṣna as predicate; the sentence may be declarative in form but command divorced women to wait, or it may be literal description.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The emphasis requires the women themselves to observe the waiting period, not have someone else observe it for them, heightening the intended force.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans say the wording is itself an imperative with an omitted imperative lām.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | A literal declarative reading reconstructs ḥukm al-muṭallaqāti an yatarabbaṣna, omitting ḥukm and the maṣdar particle an; the author calls this very remote.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Tarabbaṣa takes a direct object because it means intazara, to wait for.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The apparent analysis omits the object of tarabbaṣa, understood as marriage or husbands, and treats three quruʾ as a temporal adverb.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternatively, three quruʾ itself is the direct object: they wait for three cycles to pass.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The apparent attachment makes bi-anfusihinna modify yatarabbaṣna, with bāʾ marking cause, because of themselves; this construction requires an explicit detached self-reference rather than a bound pronoun.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternatively, anfusihinna emphatically restates the attached subject nun, with an extra bāʾ allowed before nafs or ʿayn; on this parse the phrase has no syntactic governor.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:228/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The author answers that ordinary emphasis would require a separate nominative pronoun first, but the extra bāʾ makes this emphasis adjunct-like; he cites ba- phrases and al-Akhfash's report qāmū anfusahum.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p57#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Mūsā reports the Prophet’s comparison: a Qur’an reader resembles a citron with pleasant taste and scent, while a nonreader resembles a date with pleasant taste but no scent; a wicked reader is like fragrant but bitter basil, and a wicked nonreader like a bitter, scentless colocynth.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p57#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The chapter fits the report because fragrance tracks the presence of Qur’an recitation, showing the Qur’an’s superiority over speech from both righteous and wicked people.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p57#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Ibn ʿUmar reports that the Muslim community’s allotted time is like the span from afternoon prayer to sunset, after the Jews’ morning-to-noon span and the Christians’ noon-to-afternoon span; Muslims receive two qirāṭs per worker while each earlier community received one.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p57#2/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Although its era is shorter, the Muslim community surpasses earlier communities by God’s favor, as 3:110 states; the workers’ extra reward is grace, not an injustice to the earlier communities. | mentions 3:110
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p57#2/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Bahz ibn Ḥakīm reports from his father and grandfather that the Prophet said Muslims complete seventy nations and are the best and most honored before God.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p57#2/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The community’s distinction comes through the blessed Qur’an, which God made superior to, authoritative over, abrogating, and final among the revealed books.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p57#2/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Earlier scriptures came down all at once, but the Qur’an came in stages according to events; each descent was like the arrival of one earlier book, reflecting special care for it and its Messenger.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p57#2/r8] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The Jews’ period ran from Moses to Jesus, the Christians’ from then until Muḥammad, and the Muslim community’s until the Hour; its doubled reward is God’s favor, supported by 57:28–29. | mentions 57:28, 57:29
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p606#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Divorced wives who have consummated marriages and menstruate must wait three quruʾ before they may marry again.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p606#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الأئمة الأربعة | reports | The four imams hold that an enslaved woman waits two quruʾ, half the free woman's term; a quruʾ cannot be divided, so the count is completed as two.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p606#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عائشة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report says an enslaved woman's divorce count is two and her waiting period is two menstruations; Ibn Kathir calls its transmitter Mzahir extremely weak, and al-Daraqutni says the correct version is al-Qasim's own statement.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p606#2/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عمر وعمر بن الخطاب | reports | Ibn Majah transmits a raised report from Ibn Umar, but al-Daraqutni prefers Salim and Nafi's version as Ibn Umar's own view, similarly reported from Umar; they say no Companion's disagreement was known.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p606#2/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن سيرين وبعض أهل الظاهر | rejects | Some early scholars say enslaved women have the free woman's waiting period because the verse is general and menstruation is a natural bodily process common to both; Ibn Abd al-Barr reports and weakens this view.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p606#2/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أسماء بنت يزيد بن السكن الأنصارية | reports | Asma says she was the first divorced woman for whom a waiting period was established when this verse was revealed; Ibn Abi Hatim calls this report strange by this chain.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p607/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو بكر بن عبد الرحمن | reports | Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman says every jurist he knew held Aisha's view that quruʾ are intervals of purity.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p607/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar says a woman is clear of her husband once she enters the blood of her third menstrual period; Malik says this is the established practice in his community.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p607/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس، وزيد بن ثابت، وسالم، والقاسم، وعروة، وسليمان بن يسار، وأبو بكر بن عبد الرحمن، وأبان بن عثمان، وعطاء، وقتادة، والزهري وغيرهم | reports | These authorities, and Malik, al-Shafi'i, Dawud, Abu Thawr, and one report from Ahmad, count quruʾ as purity; the purity in which divorce is pronounced counts among the three. | mentions 65:1
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p607/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | For the purity-view jurists, the waiting period ends when the third menstruation begins, and the shortest time a woman can truthfully report is 32 days and two moments.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p607/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الأعشى | reports | Abu Ubayd and others cite al-Aʿsha's poem as evidence for quruʾ meaning intervals of purity, describing wives' purity days lost to their husbands' campaigning.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p607/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الثوري ومن وافقه | reports | The second view takes quruʾ as menstruations: the waiting period ends only when the third period finishes, with some requiring a ritual bath; the shortest asserted duration is 33 days and one moment.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p607/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · علقمة عن عمر وابن مسعود | reports | A woman whose husband had divorced her asks about remarriage after her bleeding stopped but before she could pray; Ibn Masud says she remains his wife until prayer is lawful, and Umar agrees.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p608/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو بكر وعمر وعثمان وعلي وابن عباس ومجاهد وغيرهم | reports | Many early authorities count quruʾ as menstruations; this is the Hanafi position, the stronger report from Ahmad, and the views of al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, and others; senior Companions are cited in support.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p608/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · فاطمة بنت أبي حبيش عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report tells Fatima to stop praying during her quruʾ, which would plainly mean menstruation if authentic; Abu Hatim calls its transmitter Mundhir ibn al-Mughira unknown, though Ibn Hibban lists him among trustworthy narrators.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p608/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن جرير | reports | Ibn Jarir defines quruʾ as the appointed time for a regularly recurring thing to arrive or depart; this allows the word to cover both menstruation and purity, a shared-word analysis adopted by some legal theorists.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p608/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الأصمعي وأبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Al-A

sma'i says quruʾ means a time; Abu Amr says Arabs use it for menstruation, purity, and both together.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p608/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو عمر بن عبد البر | reports | Ibn Abd al-Barr says Arab linguists and jurists agree that quruʾ can mean either menstruation or purity; their disagreement is which sense the verse intends.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p609#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Women have rights over men comparable to men's rights over them; each spouse should discharge the other's due fairly.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p609#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · جابر عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In the Farewell Pilgrimage sermon, the Prophet tells men to fear God concerning women, notes the marital trust, sets household and sexual obligations, and requires food and clothing for wives according to customary standards; Muslim records the report.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p609#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · معاوية بن حيدة عن أبيه عن جده عن النبي | reports | Asked about a wife's rights, the Prophet says to feed and clothe her as oneself, not strike her face or insult her, and not abandon her except within the home.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p609#2/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says he likes to adorn himself for his wife as he likes her to adorn herself for him, citing this verse; al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim transmit it.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p609/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس وابن عمر ومجاهد والشعبي وغيرهم | reports | What divorced women may not conceal in their wombs means pregnancy or menstruation, according to Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Hakam ibn Utayba, and others.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p609/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The warning makes the woman's truthful report authoritative because she alone normally knows whether she is pregnant or menstruating and proof is usually unavailable; she must not lie to shorten or lengthen the waiting period for advantage.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p609/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | A husband may take back his wife during her waiting period if he seeks reconciliation and good; this applies to revocable divorces.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p609/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | At this verse's revelation, a husband could take back a wife even after a hundred divorces; the next verse's limit of three created irrevocable as well as revocable divorces, so this passage does not fit the legal-theory example of a pronoun restricting an earlier general term. | mentions 2:229
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p610/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Men have a degree in virtue, status, being obeyed, financial provision, managing interests, and merit in this world and the next; Ibn Kathir links this to 4:34. | mentions 4:34
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p610/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | God is mighty in requiting those who disobey and oppose His command, and wise in His command, law, and decree.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p66/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Kabsha al-Anmārī reports the Prophet’s comparison of four people: the knowledgeable wealthy person who spends rightly and the knowledgeable poor person who wishes to do the same share reward; the wealthy wrongdoer and the poor person who wishes to do the same share sin. [BIQAI-FULL:v1p427/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | prefers | The author argues that quruʾ, masculine in form with a feminine numeral, fits purity; the feminine noun menstruation takes a masculine numeral, supporting his preference.

[BURSEVI:v1p289#3/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The disagreement changes the waiting period: al-Shāfiʿī's is shorter, while Abū Ḥanīfa's is longer; for the latter, the remaining purity counts and the period ends only after the relevant menstruation finishes.
[BURSEVI:v1p289#3/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The divorced women intended are free women who menstruate and whose marriages were consummated; nonconsummated women have no waiting period, pregnant or nonmenstruating women count by months or childbirth, and an enslaved woman's period is two cycles or two months.

[BURSEVI:v1p289#3/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The declarative form functions as a command: they are to wait.

[BURSEVI:v1p289#3/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Quruʾ, plural of qarʾ, is an Arabic word with opposite senses, both purity and menstruation, like shafaq for redness and whiteness.
[BURSEVI:v1p289#3/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أبو حنيفة وأصحابه | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions take quruʾ as menstruations: since months replace cycles when menstruation ceases, menstruation must be the original measure. | mentions 65:4
[BURSEVI:v1p289#3/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī argues quruʾ means periods of purity, reading the timing phrase in 65:1 to rule out menstruation as the time for divorce. | mentions 65:1
[BURSEVI:v1p290/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | They must not conceal pregnancy or menstruation, for doing so could deny the husband's child or revocation rights, hasten separation, or lead to abortion; a woman might hide menstruation to secure a divorce during purity.
