[BURSEVI:v1p290/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Belief in God and the Last Day, when punishment follows, should prevent concealment; the warning is severe, but the prohibition applies equally to believing and unbelieving women.
[BURSEVI:v1p290/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Baʿl originally means lord or owner; a husband is called baʿl because he manages his wife, while baʿūla is a feminine collective plural, with tāʾ marking its collective femininity.
[BURSEVI:v1p290/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Calling a man baʿl after an explicit divorce signals that the marriage bond and permissibility remain; this concerns revocably divorced women, not irrevocably divorced women whose husbands lack return rights.
[BURSEVI:v1p291#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Men have an added degree of rights and merit over women, including differences in reason and religion; here the relevant superiority has two aspects.
[BURSEVI:v1p291#2/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | A report says that a woman who dies while her husband is pleased with her enters Paradise; it is cited in Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn.
[BURSEVI:v1p291#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | First, the husband's rights are greater: he may divorce and revoke during the waiting period, while his wife owes obedience and cannot fast voluntarily or leave home without his permission; her rights include dowry, support, and freedom from harm.
[BURSEVI:v1p291#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says both spouses receive the same marital pleasures, while the man's added merit is the care and financial duties he assumes for her.
[BURSEVI:v1p291#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The degree can mean the husband's compassionate responsibilities: dowry, maintenance, housing, protection, care for her interests, and shielding her from harm.
[BURSEVI:v1p291#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that, were prostration to a person permitted, he would command a wife to prostrate to her husband because God magnified his right over her.
[BURSEVI:v1p291#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The verse links to 4:34, where men's guardianship is tied to divine favor and their spending; the added duties make a wife's service in the home more emphatically obligatory. | mentions 4:34
[BURSEVI:v1p291#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God is mighty to punish those who violate His rules, and wise: His laws contain wisdom and benefits.
[BURSEVI:v1p291#2/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Marriage succeeds when both spouses honor each other's rights and improve their shared life through children, upbringing, kind treatment, home care, and household management.
[BURSEVI:v1p291#2/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | A report calls a woman's good service to her husband her jihad.
[BURSEVI:v1p291/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | A husband's right to return his wife to marriage exists only during the waiting period and ends when it expires.
[BURSEVI:v1p291/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Aḥaqq here means 'rightful' rather than comparative: outsiders have no right to the women, and a wife's refusal does not invalidate her husband's return.
[BURSEVI:v1p291/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Husbands should return wives to reconcile and treat them well, not to harm them; the intention is exhortation and a warning against abuse, not a condition for a legally valid return.
[BURSEVI:v1p291/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | In pre-Islamic practice, a man might return a wife near the end of her waiting period and divorce her again later to prolong it and harm her.
[BURSEVI:v1p291/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | After establishing that return should benefit a wife, the verse sets out reciprocal rights between spouses.
[BURSEVI:v1p291/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Each spouse owes the other rights recognized by religious law and custom; equivalence means equal binding force and claim, not identical kinds of rights—for example, a husband owes dowry, maintenance, and housing.
[BURSEVI:v1p292/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says he adorns himself for his wife just as she adorns herself for him, treating adornment as a mutual right.
[BURSEVI:v1p292/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | A saying compares a woman to a dove that flies once its wings grow, warning that a husband who dresses his wife may find her unwilling to stay home.
[BURSEVI:v1p292/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | An anecdote has a man boast that no evil entered his house; a sage asks how his wife entered it.
[BURSEVI:v1p292/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · السعدي | reports | Al-Saʿdī's couplet praises a good woman as a source of comfort and asks God for protection from a bad woman.
[BURSEVI:v1p292/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعضهم | reports | An unattributed couplet says a woman's chastity lies in her beauty and that display is forbidden unless lawful.
[BURSEVI:v1p292/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | A pious Israelite's wife asked to become the most beautiful woman, then left him for rulers; his prayer turned her into a monkey, and his final prayer restored her, wasting all three granted requests.
[BURSEVI:v1p292/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The waiting period of divorced women symbolizes God's patience with servants who sever their bond: He delays turning away, allowing time for heedlessness to lift, love to stir, and repentance and return to arise.
[BURSEVI:v1p292/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Divine grace calls the repentant seeker to leave the self and come back, and urges anyone seeking success to remain at God's threshold continually.

[ALUSI-FULL:v2p132/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الحنفية | reports | Some Hanafis argue that if qurūʾ meant purity, the numeral three would be defeated because the common divorce period contains two full purities and part of a third.

[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r17] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The verse uses elegant ihtibāk ellipsis: each half supplies the omitted reciprocal phrase in the other, conveying mutual rights and duties.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r18] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The likeness is equality in obligation, not identical kinds of acts; a husband need not mirror cooking or laundry but owes what befits men.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r19] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عمرو بن الأحوص | reports | A report from the Prophet, transmitted by al-Tirmidhi (who grades it sound), al-Nasaʾi, and Ibn Majah, lists wives' rights to kind treatment, clothing, and food, and husbands' right to sexual fidelity and household boundaries.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | One parsing treats the faith clause as a condition with an omitted result, meaning they must not conceal; the following prohibition supplies its cause.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r20] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says he likes to adorn himself for his wife as he likes her to adorn herself for him, citing this verse.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r21] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Jurists include among wives' rights that a husband not hasten intercourse before she has satisfied her need.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r22] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The degree denotes an additional right for men, since their rights concern the women themselves.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r23] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another explanation makes the degree an honor and merit: men maintain and protect women, share marriage's aims, and uniquely bear care and expenses.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r24] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib says daraja denotes a rank, especially one conceived as ascent and elevated status.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r25] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الكشف | reports | Al-Kashf traces the root to gradual, measured movement; a stair rises by stages, unlike descent or level walking, and the term extends to progression and divine leading on.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r26] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The explicit noun al-rijāl replaces a pronoun to highlight manhood as the quality associated with the stated distinction.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r27] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Almighty means that God can punish those who violate these rulings; Wise means He knows the outcomes and interests behind His legislation, and the closing warns and encourages.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Alusi objects that the proposed ellipsis makes the command explain itself, or oddly links future nonconcealment to past faith if read as a statement.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says buʿūla is the plural of baʿl, like ʿamm/ʿumūma and faḥl/fuḥūla; its feminine marker is emphatic, and these plurals are lexical rather than analogical.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · القاموس | reports | The Qamus defines baʿl as husband, lord, master, or owner; baʿla can denote a wife, and also a rain-fed palm.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib derives the husband sense from the rain-fed palm that stands on its roots, by analogy to a husband remaining with his wife.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib also relates baʿl to intercourse, and explains a baffled man as standing still like a palm that does not move.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The choice of baʿūla hints that restoration to marriage is originally effected by intercourse; alternatively it is a source meaning good conjugal companionship or stands for its omitted people.
[ALUSI-FULL:v2p134/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The husbands' right to restore the wives during the waiting period applies to revocable divorce, as the following verse indicates. | mentions 2:229
[ELMALILI:2:228/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The general category of divorced women is qualified by other texts to exclude menopausal, pregnant, unconsummated, minor, and enslaved women.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Baʿl can name an idol once worshipped or, with the sense of height, a lord, owner, master, husband, or wife; attached to men it means wives, and to women it means their current husbands.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | During the waiting period, husbands who divorced revocably retain their status and have the strongest right to take their wives back; even if she objects, the husband's decision prevails.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The return is permitted when the husbands seek reconciliation rather than harm or separation; this is legally shown by having issued a revocable rather than irrevocable divorce.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A husband's hidden intention to prolong the waiting period in order to harm his wife merits divine accountability under 2:225. | mentions 2:225
[ELMALILI:2:228/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Women have reciprocal rights against men according to recognized good custom, illustrated by verses on kind treatment, fair retention or release, support, guardianship, dowry, and equitable marital treatment. | mentions 4:19, 2:229, 2:233, 4:34, 4:4, 4:20, 4:129
[ELMALILI:2:228/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The general rule on reciprocal rights entails that if no dower was named at marriage, a dower matching her peers is still due.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The husband's additional degree corresponds to his duties to protect, manage, and support the family and carry its expenses; he must not abuse this distinction.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God is mighty and wise: He punishes those who oppose His rulings, which are filled with wisdom and benefits.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Qurūʾ, plural of qarʾ, has the opposed senses of menstruation and purity, making it a shared, ambiguous term whose intended sense must be determined.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · İmam Mâlik ve Şâfiî | reports | Mālik and Shāfiʿī interpret qurūʾ as periods of purity.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Hazret-i Âişe | reports | A report from ʿĀʾisha, cited from Abū Dāwūd and Tirmidhī, attributes to the Prophet that a slave woman's divorce is two divorces and her waiting period is two menstruations; Elmalılı uses it to support the menstrual sense.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · İbn Ömer | reports | A second Prophetic report, narrated by Imām Shāfiʿī from Ibn ʿUmar, likewise supports the menstrual interpretation.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | Elmalılı adopts the Ḥanafī interpretation of qurūʾ as menstruation, supported by the purpose of establishing that the womb is clear and by further juristic proofs.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Hulefâ-i Râşidîn, Âbâdile, Übey b. Ka‘b, Muâz b. Cebel, Ebü’d-Derdâ, Ubâde b. Sâmit, Zeyd b. Sâbit, Ebû Mûse’l-Eş‘arî ve Ma‘bed-i Cühenî | reports | The same interpretation of qurūʾ as menstruation is also attributed to these early authorities.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A free, adult divorced woman must wait until she has completed three menstrual periods.
[ELMALILI:2:228/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A woman must not conceal menstruation or pregnancy; if she believes in God and the Last Day she should disclose it truthfully, and her statement governs this matter.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p393/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | بعولة is the plural of بعل, ‘husband’; بعل originally meant ‘master’ and is an old Semitic word. The Canaanite/Phoenician deity Baal is named at 37:125. | mentions 37:125
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p393/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Husband was called بعل because he held authority over the marital bond and was regarded as a woman’s owner and master. [IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p393/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The Quran usually calls spouses زَوْج; exceptions occur in accounts of earlier peoples, as at 11:72, or when recalling male authority, as at 4:128 and here, where the husband has the right of return. | mentions 11:72, 4:128
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p393/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · قيل | reports | Another view derives بعل from ‘male’: the deity Baal symbolizes masculine power, and a tree that grows without irrigation is also called بعل.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p393/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The waiting period gives men room to regret and seek reconciliation, as 65:1 says, ‘perhaps God will bring about something after that’; this resembles the rule of īlāʾ. | mentions 65:1
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p393/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | During the waiting period divorced women are between the status of wives and strangers; calling their former husbands بَعُولة is a transparent metaphor based on their prior status, like continuing to call grown wards ‘orphans’ at 4:2. | mentions 4:2
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p395#2/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The condition ‘if they intend reconciliation’ exhorts husbands to seek repair; it does not restrict the right to return.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p395#2/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | لَهُنّ cannot refer to the nearest ‘divorced women,’ who no longer have mutual marital rights; it refers to wives implied by ‘returning them.’ Accordingly الرجال means their husbands, as ‘the man of a woman’ means her husband, like ‘his wife’ at 11:71 and 11:81. | mentions 11:71, 11:81
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p395#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Alternatively, the pronoun may refer to wives in 2:226: since unjustified īlāʾ harms their rights, the general rule follows that specific context. [IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p395#2/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The reminder of equal rights fits the preceding mention of īlāʾ, which can involve husbands asserting control over the marital bond at women’s expense. | mentions 2:226
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p395#2/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The verse uses symmetrical ellipsis: its full sense is that women have against men rights like the rights men have against women, with each half elided because the other supplies it.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p395#2/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Women’s rights are stated first because men’s claims over women were long familiar and accepted, while women’s rights were neglected or left to a wife’s standing with her husband; Islam established them, and this verse is a central foundation.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p395/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | ذلك points to the waiting period’s duration: husbands may return their wives during the three quruʾ, not afterward. The verse legislates reconciliation while the divorce waiting period lasts.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p395/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | He says the verse both establishes reconciliation and urges divorced husbands to pursue it: since one or both spouses may want reunion, men are urged to overlook causes of divorce, being more likely to judge patiently while women are more prone to anger and refusal.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p395/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | رد was discussed at 2:217; here it means returning to married life, or reconciliation. | mentions 2:217
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p395/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · مالك | reports | Malik treats ‘returning’ literally, supporting the view that divorce legally severs the marriage bond.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p395/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أبو حنيفة ومن وافقوه | reports | Abu Hanifa and his followers read ‘return’ figuratively: during the waiting period the bond is already on a path to dissolution at its end, and reconciliation turns it back from that course.
[TABATABAI:2:228#2/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Baʿūla is the plural of baʿl, a male spouse while the couple remains married; its associations of height, strength, and steadiness underlie uses for a rider, elevated land, an idol, and a mature palm.
[TABATABAI:2:228#2/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The pronoun refers to the divorced women, but the return right applies only to revocably divorced women, during the waiting period, not irrevocably divorced women.
[TABATABAI:2:228#2/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The condition requires the husband to intend reconciliation and reform, barring return intended to injure the woman, as the following verse also forbids. | mentions 2:231
[TABATABAI:2:228#2/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The comparative ‘more entitled’ implies a comparison with other suitors, but only the first husband can actually resume the marriage; its implied sense is ‘more entitled to them than others.’
[TABATABAI:2:228#2/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The comparative entitlement itself confirms that the rule concerns revocable divorces, since irrevocable divorce permits no return.
[TABATABAI:2:228#2/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | This verse addresses consummated marriages of menstruating women who are not pregnant; other verses govern unconsummated marriages, minors, menopausal women, and pregnant women.
[TABATABAI:2:228#2/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Maʿrūf is what people recognize through the acquired taste of their social life; under Islam’s natural order it also embraces reason, religious law, good character, and proper etiquette.
[TABATABAI:2:228#2/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The passage repeats maʿrūf twelve times to ensure divorce and related conduct follow sound, natural standards.
[TABATABAI:2:228#2/r9] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Natural social order requires equal rights and duties, while recognizing each person’s distinct contribution and status; Islam gives women what it places upon them while preserving their social weight in marriage and procreation.
[TABATABAI:2:228-231/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The degree is a rank that qualifies the preceding equality: women receive like obligations and rights while men retain their degree over them; he promises fuller treatment later.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#11/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أسماء بنت يزيد بن السكن الأنصارية | reports | Asma says she was divorced during the Prophet’s time when divorced women had no waiting period; the verse established the first divorce waiting period.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#11/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · ربيعة الرأي | reports | Rabiʿa holds that the Qur’anic qurūʾ are the periods of purity between menstruations, not menstruation itself.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#11/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو جعفر | reports | Imam al-Baqir says Rabiʿa’s purity interpretation came from Ali; the Imams reject the popular attribution that Ali counted menstruations as qurūʾ.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#11/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو جعفر | reports | For a divorce pronounced during purity without intercourse and witnessed by two just men, al-Baqir says the waiting period ends when the third menstruation begins.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#12/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says several chains report from Ali that qurūʾ means periods of purity, as the preceding narration states.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#12/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | A report cited from al-Shafiʿi and other Sunni authorities attributes to Ali the view that the wife may be taken back until she bathes after the third menstruation.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#12/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · زيد بن ثابت، عبد الله بن عمر، عائشة | reports | The purity interpretation is also attributed to Zayd ibn Thabit, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, and ʿAʾisha.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#12/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · جعفر الصادق | reports | Al-Ṣadiq interprets what God created in women’s wombs as pregnancy and menstruation.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#12/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | reports | Tafsīr al-Qummī says God entrusted women with three matters: purity, menstruation, and pregnancy.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#12/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · جعفر الصادق | reports | Al-Qummī transmits al-Ṣadiq’s statement that men’s rights over women are greater than women’s rights over men.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#12/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | This report does not conflict with equality in the way reciprocal rights are established, as the commentary explained earlier.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#19/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The author compares human use of domestic animals: people treat their lives as subordinate to human needs and recognize claims against them only as property claims belonging to the owner.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#19/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | He says women in many societies likewise lived dependently, treated as made for men, without independent lives or rights, under the absolute guardianship of fathers and then husbands.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#19/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The author describes men as controlling women’s bodies, marriage, labor, and property, while women were required to obey and perform domestic and arduous work without independence.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#19/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | He notes that customs varied by people and environment, including a reported tribe where a woman resumed household work immediately after childbirth while her husband rested in her bed.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#2/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | These two rulings uniquely invoke belief in God and the Last Day because monotheism calls people to unity and connection rather than separation.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#2/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The discourse shifts between singular and plural: rulings address the whole community, while non-ruling clauses sometimes address the Prophet directly, preserving the speech's structure and his central role. | mentions

 2:229
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#20/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | In pre-Islamic societies governed mainly by inherited custom, including China, India, ancient Egypt, and Iran, women's status followed local practice rather than scripture or codified law.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#20/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Women lacked independent will and action, had no public role in government or adjudication, and were expected both to work alongside men and to manage the home and obey them.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#20/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Compared with women in less settled societies, they were generally spared killing and eating, but men could take unlimited wives, divorce them, and remarry after a wife's death.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#20/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | A woman could sometimes acquire property by inheritance, marriage, or other means, yet could not dispose of it independently.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#20/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Customs differed by region and class: some elite Iranian women could participate in property, rule, or sovereignty, and marriages among close relatives occurred.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#20/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | In China, marriage resembled purchasing the woman into subjection; women lacked inheritance and even shared meals with men, while multiple men could share one wife and children were assigned chiefly to the strongest husband.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#20/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | In India, widows could not remarry and were either burned with their husbands or left humiliated; menstruating women and what touched them were treated as impure.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#20/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Al-Tabataba'i summarizes these societies as treating women like an inferior being between animal and human, useful as a weak dependent who must remain under guardianship.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#21/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Some societies, including the Chaldeans, Romans, and Greeks, lived under written law or scripture, unlike the customs-based societies discussed earlier.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#21/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Under Hammurabi's law, a wife was subordinate; disobedience could lead to expulsion or treatment as a concubine, and proven wasteful household management could lead to drowning.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#21/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Rome began codifying civil law around 400 BCE and gradually expanded it; household heads exercised authority over domestic affairs.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#21/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The Roman paterfamilias was treated as a household deity and had unrestricted command over wife and children, even authority to kill them without challenge.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#21/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Roman women had less standing than dependent male children: they could not complain, transact, or participate in public life, while men, including adopted sons, could be authorized to act independently.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#21/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | In Greek and Roman-style households, formal kinship and inheritance linked men; women lacked official kinship even with mothers, daughters, sisters, husbands, and sons, although natural kinship still existed and could shape marriage and household authority.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#22/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | A woman's life was controlled by her father or husband: he could sell, give, lend, punish, control her property, arrange her marriage, and divorce her.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#22/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Greek household organization and the subordination of women were broadly similar to the Roman pattern.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#22/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | These legal systems contradicted themselves: women were punished independently for wrongdoing but recognized or rewarded only through male guardianship, reflecting a view of them as dangerous yet necessary for reproduction and useful to men.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#22/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Because society was understood to depend on men, male descendants alone counted as true continuers of a household; adoption and having a male relative impregnate a barren man's wife were used to prevent extinction.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#22/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Greek men could have multiple wives, but only one was an official wife; the others lacked that formal status.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#23/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The Arabs lived on a hot, arid peninsula, mostly as nomadic raiding tribes connected to Persia, Rome, Abyssinia, and Sudan; their customs were mainly uncivilized but borrowed regional practices.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#23/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Arab women generally lacked independent standing, inheritance, and social honor beyond family reputation; men could have unlimited wives and divorce freely.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#23/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Female infanticide began among Banū Tamīm after the capture of their daughters in a conflict with al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir, then spread to other Arabs.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#23/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Arabs regarded a daughter as a disgrace and hid her birth, while celebrating sons even when obtained by adoption or affiliation; rival chiefs sometimes claimed the same child.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#23/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Some elite households allowed women, especially daughters, a say in choosing marriage, resembling Iranian aristocratic custom.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#23/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Arab treatment combined urban restrictions on women's rights and public roles with the coercion of barbarian societies; it arose from power over the weak, not household-head worship.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#23/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Arab men and women worshipped idols tied to tribal preferences, including stars, angels imagined as God's daughters, and objects such as stones and wood.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#24/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | reports | A satirical verse mocked Banū Ḥanīfa for worshipping an idol made from date paste and then eating it during famine.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#24/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Arabs might replace a stone idol with a better stone, or make an idol by pouring milk over a handful of soil and worship it.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#24/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Al-Tabataba'i says deprivation and suffering weakened women's thought and made them susceptible to strange superstitions about events, recorded in historical works.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#24/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | His first conclusion is that societies viewed women as animal-like or as deficient, unsafe human beings if freed from dependence; he associates the harsher view with uncivilized peoples.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#24/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Second, women were excluded from society's structure, viewed instead as a necessary condition of it or as captive dependents exploited by dominant society.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#24/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Third, women were denied nearly all rights except to the extent that men responsible for them could benefit.
[TABATABAI:2:228-242#24/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Fourth, relations with women rested on the strong exploiting the weak; settled societies additionally claimed that women's nature made them incapable of independence and dangerous if trusted.
